2020.Q3:
### Financial Insights

1. **Third quarter 2020 net income declined 34% year-over-year to \$100 million, pressured by metal spread compression and COVID-19 impacts.**  
   Steel Dynamics reported net income attributable to the company of \$100.1 million in Q3 2020, down from \$151 million in Q3 2019. Adjusted net income excluding \$11 million of costs related to the Sinton, Texas flat roll mill construction was \$108 million. Consolidated operating income fell 32% to \$155.9 million compared to Q3 2019. The year-to-date net income for the first nine months of 2020 was \$363 million, a 34% decrease from the same period in 2019, reflecting lower operating income and higher interest expenses due to refinancing in June 2020 [8-K 2020-10-21; 10-Q 2020-11-09].

2. **Net sales in Q3 2020 decreased 8% year-over-year to \$2.3 billion, driven by lower average selling prices despite a modest shipment decline.**  
   The company’s net sales declined from \$2.5 billion in Q3 2019 to \$2.33 billion in Q3 2020. Steel operations net sales fell 12% due to a 9% decrease in average selling prices and a 2% decrease in shipments. The average external steel selling price dropped \$75 per ton (9%) year-over-year to \$734 per ton [8-K 2020-10-21; 10-Q 2020-11-09].

3. **Adjusted EBITDA for Q3 2020 was \$238 million, down from \$315 million in Q3 2019, reflecting margin pressures despite higher shipments compared to Q2 2020.**  
   The decline in EBITDA reflects metal spread compression, primarily from lower selling prices lagging scrap cost reductions, and COVID-19 related demand disruptions in Q2, partially reversed in Q3 [8-K 2020-10-21; 10-Q 2020-11-09].

4. **The company maintained strong liquidity with cash and equivalents of \$1.27 billion and total liquidity of \$2.5 billion as of September 30, 2020, despite repurchasing \$107 million of common stock year-to-date.**  
   Long-term debt remained stable at approximately \$2.64 billion. Interest expense decreased sequentially but remained elevated due to refinancing costs incurred in June 2020 [8-K 2020-10-21; 10-Q 2020-11-09].

### Operations Insights

5. **Steel operations shipments declined 2% year-over-year in Q3 2020 but increased 8% sequentially from Q2 2020 as industrial activity resumed post-COVID-19 shutdowns.**  
   The company shipped 2.31 million tons externally in Q3 2020, down 2% from Q3 2019 but up 8% from Q2 2020. Utilization of steel mills was 85% of production capability in Q3, with the flat roll group running at 99%, notably above the domestic industry average of 64% [8-K 2020-10-21; 10-Q 2020-11-09].

6. **Average steel selling prices fell 9% year-over-year to \$734 per ton, while average ferrous scrap cost per ton melted decreased 6% to \$259, resulting in an 11% contraction in metal spread.**  
   The metal spread—the difference between steel mill selling prices and ferrous scrap costs—declined due to the sharper drop in steel prices relative to scrap prices, compressing steel operations margins. This drove a 41% decrease in steel operations operating income to \$139.5 million in Q3 2020 versus Q3 2019 [10-Q 2020-11-09].

7. **Metals recycling operations reversed a Q2 loss to generate \$15 million operating income in Q3 2020 on stronger scrap flows and higher ferrous scrap prices.**  
   Improved scrap availability followed the reopening of automotive and other steel-consuming industries. Ferrous scrap average selling prices increased 13% year-over-year in Q3 2020, lifting metals recycling operating income from a loss of \$6 million in Q2 to a \$15 million profit in Q3 [8-K 2020-10-21; 10-Q 2020-11-09].

8. **Steel fabrication operations achieved record quarterly operating income of \$39.2 million in Q3 2020, up 11% year-over-year on a 6% shipment increase despite a 6% decline in average selling prices.**  
   Fabrication shipments reached a record 179,000 tons in Q3 2020, supported by resilient non-residential construction demand. The metal spread expanded slightly due to steel input costs declining 11% year-over-year, partially offsetting the selling price decrease [8-K 2020-10-21; 10-Q 2020-11-09].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

9. **The company’s flat roll steel segment saw pricing lag recovery relative to cost reductions due to contract arrangements, contributing to metal spread compression and lower steel operations earnings.**  
   The average external product selling price for steel operations decreased by \$21 sequentially from Q2 to Q3 2020 to \$734 per ton, while ferrous scrap cost dropped \$7 sequentially to \$259 per ton melted. This lag in price recovery versus input cost reduction compressed margins in the flat roll business [8-K 2020-10-21].

10. **Steel Dynamics is progressing with construction of a new \$1.9 billion electric arc furnace (EAF) flat roll steel mill in Sinton, Texas, on schedule for mid-2021 start-up, with \$11 million of related costs expensed in Q3 2020.**  
    The facility is designed for product size and quality capabilities beyond existing EAF flat roll producers, targeting regional steel-consuming markets and import displacement. The company has signed long-term agreements with three customers to co-locate on site, expected to consume 800,000 to 1 million tons annually. The recent acquisition of Zimmer, a Mexican metals recycler, supports raw material strategy for this facility [8-K 2020-10-21].

### Labor Insights

11. **Profit sharing expense declined 34% year-over-year in Q3 2020 to \$11.8 million, reflecting lower pretax earnings amid the pandemic.**  
    Profit sharing represents 8% of pretax earnings; the reduced expense corresponds with the drop in earnings [8-K 2020-10-21; 10-Q 2020-11-09].

### Corporate and Risk Insights

12. **The company completed a \$750 million debt offering in October 2020, issuing \$350 million of 1.65% notes due 2027 and \$400 million of 3.25% notes due 2050, as part of its capital structure management.**  
    This refinancing followed a June 2020 refinancing of senior notes contributing to higher interest expenses year-to-date. The notes were registered under a Form S-3 registration statement filed with the SEC [8-K 2020-10-09; 10-Q 2020-11-09].

### Wrap Up

Steel Dynamics’ third quarter 2020 results show a recovery in shipments and industrial activity following severe COVID-19 disruptions in Q2, with steel mill utilization rising to 85% and fabrication hitting record shipments. However, earnings were pressured by a 9% year-over-year decline in average steel selling prices and metal spread compression, as steel prices lagged input cost reductions, particularly in the flat roll segment. Metals recycling improved substantially, reversing prior losses due to stronger scrap flows and higher ferrous scrap prices. The company sustained strong liquidity and proceeded with its \$1.9 billion Sinton flat roll mill project on schedule, reflecting ongoing capital investments aimed at geographic and product diversification.

Management highlighted continued resilience in automotive and construction markets, though energy remains weak. The recent debt issuance and refinancing increased interest expenses but supported liquidity. Profit sharing expenses declined in line with earnings. Overall, Steel Dynamics navigated a challenging operating environment with mixed financial outcomes, balancing operational recovery against persistent margin pressures and ongoing strategic investments.
2020.Q4:
### Financial Insights

1. **Fourth quarter 2020 net sales rose sequentially to \$2.6 billion, with net income of \$188 million, partly offset by refinancing and construction costs.**  
   Steel Dynamics reported Q4 2020 net sales of \$2.6 billion, up from \$2.33 billion in Q3 2020. Net income was \$188 million, or \$0.89 per diluted share, improving from \$100 million in Q3 2020. Adjusted net income excluding \$11 million in additional financing costs related to an October 2020 refinancing and approximately \$15 million in costs associated with the Sinton Texas Flat Roll Steel Mill construction was \$205 million, or \$0.97 per diluted share [8-K 2021-01-28; 8-K 2020-12-21].  
   For the full year 2020, net sales totaled \$9.6 billion, down 8% from \$10.5 billion in 2019. Net income attributable to Steel Dynamics decreased 18% to \$551 million from \$671 million in 2019. Operating income declined 14% to \$847 million from \$987 million in 2019 [10-K 2021-03-01; 8-K 2021-01-28].

2. **Operating income doubled sequentially in Q4 2020 to \$259 million driven by steel operations' metal spread expansion and strong demand.**  
   Q4 2020 operating income was \$259 million, significantly higher than \$156 million reported in Q3 2020. The increase was primarily due to steel operations segment operating income rising to \$298 million from \$144 million sequentially, reflecting a \$80 per ton increase in average steel selling price to \$814 per ton and only a \$20 per ton increase in ferrous scrap cost to \$279 per ton. Metals recycling operating income increased 75% sequentially to \$27 million due to stronger scrap volumes and prices [8-K 2021-01-28; 8-K 2020-10-21].

3. **Annual steel shipments declined marginally by 1%, but steel fabrication shipments reached a record 666,000 tons in 2020.**  
   Steel operations segment shipments were 9.72 million tons in 2020, down 1% from 9.84 million tons in 2019. External shipments declined 2% to 9.26 million tons. Steel fabrication shipments set a record at 666,000 tons [8-K 2021-01-28; 10-K 2021-03-01].

4. **Metal spread compression in 2020 reduced profitability despite strong shipment volumes and record fabrication shipments.**  
   Average steel selling prices for the steel operations segment decreased 8% year-over-year (down \$69 per ton), while ferrous scrap costs declined less sharply by \$25 per ton, leading to a 2% decrease in metal spread. This compression was the primary cause of the 14% decline in operating income for the year. Steel fabrication operating income increased slightly to a record \$121 million due to higher shipments offsetting lower metal spread [10-K 2021-03-01].

5. **Capital expenditures surged with \$928 million spent in 2020 on the Southwest-Sinton Flat Roll Division, expected to begin operations mid-2021.**  
   The company invested heavily in the new Sinton Texas Flat Roll Steel Mill, with \$928 million spent in 2020 and outstanding commitments of \$561 million as of year-end. The facility is planned to start mid-2021. This investment is the largest ongoing capital project and has generated construction-related costs affecting earnings [10-K 2021-03-01; 8-K 2020-12-21; 8-K 2020-10-21].

6. **Liquidity remained strong with approximately \$1.37 billion in cash and equivalents at year-end 2020, supporting ongoing investments and refinancing activities.**  
   The company held \$1.37 billion in cash and equivalents at December 31, 2020, essentially flat with 2019 despite significant capital spending. The October 2020 refinancing added \$11 million in financing costs in Q4 but positions the company for financial flexibility [10-K 2021-03-01; 8-K 2021-01-28].

### Operations Insights

7. **Steel operations utilization was high, with flat roll mills operating at 99% of capacity in Q3 2020, supporting shipment volumes despite the pandemic.**  
   During Q3 2020, the flat roll steel group operated at 99% capacity, well above the domestic industry average of 64%. This high utilization supported shipment volumes that were only 1% lower year-over-year for 2020 despite COVID-19 disruptions in Q2 [8-K 2020-10-21; 10-K 2021-03-01].

8. **Raw material costs for ferrous scrap rose sequentially in Q4 2020 but remained below steel selling price increases, improving metal spread.**  
   Ferrous scrap cost per ton melted increased \$20 sequentially in Q4 2020 to \$279 per ton, while steel selling prices increased \$80 per ton to \$814. This contributed to metal spread expansion and higher steel operations profitability [8-K 2021-01-28].

9. **Steel fabrication earnings declined sequentially in Q4 2020 due to seasonal shipment reductions and metal spread compression but achieved record annual shipments and operating income.**  
   Fabrication operating income in Q4 2020 was lower than in Q3 due to lower seasonal shipments and compression of metal spread as steel input costs increased faster than selling prices. Nonetheless, 2020 was a record year for both shipments (666,000 tons) and operating income (\$121 million) for steel fabrication [8-K 2020-12-21; 10-K 2021-03-01].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

10. **Steel pricing recovered strongly in Q4 2020, with flat roll steel prices increasing over \$500 per ton from August through year-end, reflecting tight supply and low inventory.**  
    Steel Dynamics noted a strong increase in flat roll steel prices in the second half of 2020, driven by tight supply and historically low inventory levels in the supply chain. This pricing strength was a key driver of improved metal spread and operating income in Q4 [10-K 2021-03-01; 8-K 2021-01-28].

11. **The company secured long-term agreements with three customers to co-locate at the Sinton facility, representing 800,000 to 1 million tons of annual flat roll steel consumption.**  
    As part of its growth strategy, Steel Dynamics signed long-term agreements with three customers to co-locate at the new Sinton Texas Flat Roll Steel Mill, which is designed to target specific regional steel-consuming markets and displace imports [8-K 2020-10-21].

### Corporate and Risk Insights

12. **A \$19.4 million non-cash asset impairment charge related to noncore oil and gas joint ventures was recorded in Q4 2020, reducing net income by \$12 million.**  
    The company assessed impairment indicators due to the outlook of its noncore oil and gas joint ventures and concluded their carrying amounts were fully impaired, resulting in a non-cash charge in Q4 2020 [10-K 2021-03-01].

### Wrap Up

Steel Dynamics’ 2020 fourth quarter reflected a rebound in steel pricing and demand that drove a doubling of operating income sequentially, supported by strong utilization and metal spread expansion in steel operations. Despite COVID-19 disruptions earlier in the year, the company achieved near-record steel shipments and record steel fabrication shipments for the full year, although metal spread compression and lower average selling prices weighed on annual profitability. Capital spending on the Southwest-Sinton Flat Roll Division was substantial, with operations expected to commence mid-2021, positioning the company for strategic growth. Liquidity remained robust despite heavy investment and refinancing costs. The company also recorded a one-time impairment related to noncore oil and gas ventures.

The company’s first quarter 2021 earnings guidance suggests continued momentum with expected record quarterly earnings excluding Sinton construction costs, driven by higher flat roll steel prices and volumes. However, steel fabrication earnings are expected to decline sequentially due to the timing of backlog pricing relative to steel input cost increases. The firm anticipates April 2021 as a low point for fabrication earnings, with strong order activity continuing. No other material operational interruptions or litigation risks were disclosed for the quarter.
2020.FY:
### Financial Insights

1. **Steel Dynamics' 2020 net sales and earnings declined versus 2019 amid COVID-19 impacts but maintained strong cash flow.**  
   For the year ended December 31, 2020, Steel Dynamics reported net sales of \$9.6 billion, down 8% from \$10.5 billion in 2019. Operating income declined 14% to \$847 million from \$987 million, and net income fell 18% to \$551 million from \$671 million. Diluted earnings per share were \$2.59 in 2020 compared to \$3.04 in 2019. Despite these decreases, cash flow from operations remained robust at \$987 million, supporting liquidity and capital investments [8-K 2021-01-28; 10-K 2021-03-01].

2. **Second quarter 2020 earnings were particularly affected by COVID-19 disruptions, with a recovery in subsequent quarters.**  
   Second quarter 2020 net sales dropped to \$2.1 billion from \$2.8 billion in the prior year quarter, and net income declined sharply to \$75 million from \$194 million, reflecting temporary closures of steel-consuming businesses, especially automotive. Operating income for Q2 fell 41% sequentially due to lower selling prices and shipments. However, third quarter results showed improvement with net sales of \$2.3 billion and net income of \$100 million, as demand rebounded. Fourth quarter net sales rose to \$2.6 billion with net income of \$188 million, reflecting stronger steel shipments and pricing recovery [8-K 2020-07-22; 8-K 2020-10-21; 8-K 2021-01-28].

3. **Adjusted earnings exclude significant refinancing and mill construction costs, highlighting investment-related expenses.**  
   In 2020, Steel Dynamics incurred additional financing costs of \$11 million (Q4) and \$25 million (Q2) related to refinancing senior notes. The company also reported costs associated with constructing the Sinton, Texas Flat Roll Steel Mill, totaling approximately \$10-15 million per quarter in H2 2020 and \$927.7 million capitalized in 2020 overall. These costs reduced reported net income but were excluded in adjusted earnings calculations, which showed higher underlying profitability [8-K 2020-07-22; 8-K 2020-10-21; 8-K 2020-12-21; 10-K 2021-03-01].

4. **The company maintained quarterly dividends and repurchased stock despite challenging conditions.**  
   Steel Dynamics declared quarterly dividends of \$0.25 per share in 2020, consistent with prior years. The company repurchased \$349 million of common stock in 2019, supporting shareholder returns. Liquidity remained strong with cash and equivalents around \$1.4 billion and total liquidity near \$2.8 billion in mid-2020, supported by a \$1.2 billion unsecured revolving credit facility [8-K 2020-08-25; 10-K 2021-03-01].

### Operations Insights

5. **Steel shipments declined slightly in 2020, with a 1% drop in total shipments to 10.7 million tons and a 2% decrease in external shipments.**  
   Steel operations segment shipments totaled approximately 9.7 million tons, down 1% from 9.8 million tons in 2019. External shipments decreased 2% to 9.3 million tons. The company’s flat roll mills operated at 79% capacity in Q2 2020 amid COVID-19 shutdowns, with recovery in later quarters as steel-consuming industries resumed operations [10-K 2021-03-01; 8-K 2020-07-22].

6. **Steel operations faced metal spread compression due to falling steel prices outpacing scrap cost declines, squeezing margins.**  
   Average steel selling prices in the steel operations segment decreased by \$69 per ton (8%) in 2020 compared to 2019, while ferrous scrap costs fell by \$45 per ton. This resulted in a contraction of metal spread, the difference between steel selling prices and scrap costs, which reduced operating income. For example, year-to-date 2020 average selling prices decreased \$108 per ton to \$755, while scrap costs dropped \$45 per ton to \$264. The compression was especially pronounced in Q2 2020 [10-K 2021-03-01; 10-Q 2020-08-10].

7. **Steel fabrication shipments reached a record 666,000 tons in 2020, supporting segment profitability despite steel operations challenges.**  
   The steel fabrication platform set a shipment record with 666,000 tons in 2020, up from 644,000 tons in 2019. Operating income for fabrication was also a record, supported by a strong non-residential construction backlog. However, management noted that steel fabrication earnings in Q4 2020 were lower than Q3 due to seasonal shipment declines and metal spread compression from rising steel input costs [8-K 2021-01-28; 10-K 2021-03-01; 8-K 2020-12-21].

8. **Metals recycling operations were negatively impacted in Q2 2020 but rebounded strongly in H2 2020.**  
   Scrap generation and demand dropped sharply in Q2 2020 due to COVID-19, leading to operating losses in recycling operations. As industrial activity resumed mid-year, scrap volumes and profitability improved significantly in Q3 and Q4 2020, contributing to overall cash flow and raw material supply for steelmaking [8-K 2020-06-22; 8-K 2020-09-21].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

9. **Steel pricing experienced volatility with significant price increases in H2 2020 following low inventories and supply disruptions.**  
   After a steep drop in demand and pricing in Q2 2020, steel prices rebounded strongly from August to year-end, with flat roll steel index prices increasing over \$500 per ton. Despite this, average segment selling prices for 2020 were still down 8% year-over-year, reflecting the lag between market prices and contract pricing. The company expects continued steel price strength and strong customer demand in 2021 [10-K 2021-03-01; 8-K 2020-12-21; 8-K 2021-01-28].

10. **The company is expanding flat roll capacity with the Sinton Texas mill investment, expecting mid-2021 startup.**  
    Construction of the Southwest-Sinton Flat Roll Division began in 2019, with operations planned to commence mid-year 2021. Capital expenditures for Sinton were \$928 million in 2020 and \$205 million in 2019. The company has incurred significant start-up and construction costs in 2020, which are capitalized but impact quarterly earnings. This capacity addition aligns with the company's strategic growth plans [10-K 2021-03-01; 8-K 2020-12-21].

### Market and Capacity Insights

11. **Acquisitions continued to diversify Steel Dynamics’ product portfolio, including the August 2020 Zimmer acquisition.**  
    On August 3, 2020, Steel Dynamics acquired Zimmer for \$60 million in cash, further expanding its steel fabrication capabilities. The company also integrated United Steel Supply (USS) from March 2019, reflecting ongoing efforts to broaden its product and service offerings [10-K 2021-03-01; 8-K 2020-08-05].

### Corporate and Risk Insights

12. **COVID-19 posed operational and market risks, with temporary plant idling and demand disruptions in Q2 2020, but no labor contract expirations in 2020.**  
    The company reported temporary closures of steel-consuming businesses, especially in automotive, leading to lower shipments and earnings in Q2 2020. However, Steel Dynamics noted no collective bargaining agreements expiring during 2020 for its workforce, which comprises about 9% unionized employees. The company also highlighted risks from unexpected plant outages, raw material price volatility, and trade policy uncertainties in its SEC filings [10-K 2021-03-01; 8-K 2020-07-22].

---

### Wrap Up

Steel Dynamics’ 2020 financial and operational performance reflected significant COVID-19 disruptions, particularly in the second quarter, with a sharp decline in steel shipments, pricing, and earnings. The company managed to maintain near-record steel fabrication shipments and strong cash flow, supported by a recovering demand environment in the second half of the year and a resilient non-residential construction market. Metal spread compression due to steel price declines outpacing scrap cost reductions pressured margins, though rising steel prices late in the year indicated improving market conditions. Capital investments, notably the nearly \$1 billion Sinton flat roll mill project, continued despite the pandemic, positioning the company for capacity growth in mid-2021. Acquisitions like Zimmer broadened the company’s fabrication footprint. Risks from the pandemic, supply chain disruptions, and raw material cost volatility remain acknowledged but contained within the 2020 disclosures.

**Guidance:** For Q1 2021, Steel Dynamics projected earnings per diluted share of \$1.88 to \$1.92, or \$1.94 to \$1.98 excluding approximately \$18 million of Sinton mill construction costs. Management indicated this could represent a record earnings quarter, driven by volume and improved metal margins, despite expected lower steel fabrication earnings due to the timing of backlog pricing versus higher steel input costs. The company anticipates April 2021 as a low point for steel fabrication earnings, with strong order activity and pricing for steel joist and deck products [8-K 2021-03-19].

2021.Q1:
### Financial Insights

1. **Steel Dynamics reported record first quarter 2021 financial results, with net sales of \$3.54 billion and net income of \$431 million, more than doubling 2020's net income of \$187 million.**  
   Net sales increased 38% from \$2.58 billion in 2020Q1 to \$3.54 billion in 2021Q1. Net income attributable to Steel Dynamics rose 130% to \$430.5 million from \$187.3 million. Operating income more than doubled to \$594.2 million from \$273.7 million. Adjusted EBITDA reached a record \$664 million, up from \$356 million in 2020Q1 [8-K 2021-04-20; 10-Q 2021-04-29].

2. **Operating income growth was driven by steel operations, which saw a 121% increase to \$637 million, and metals recycling, which increased operating income by over 800% to \$50.6 million, while steel fabrication earnings declined 66% to \$9.9 million.**  
   Steel operations accounted for 71% of consolidated net sales and delivered record operating income. Metals recycling benefited from stronger scrap pricing and mill utilization. Steel fabrication faced lower earnings despite record shipments and a 17% sales increase, due to higher steel input costs compressing metal spread by 19% [10-Q 2021-04-29; 8-K 2021-04-20].

3. **Selling, general and administrative expenses increased 33% to \$149.8 million, consistent with higher sales and profitability, while profit sharing expense more than doubled to \$48.8 million reflecting 8% of pretax earnings.**  
   Interest expense decreased to \$17.3 million from \$28 million in 2020Q1, benefiting from capitalized interest on growth projects [10-Q 2021-04-29].

4. **Cash flow from operations grew to \$262 million from \$211 million year-over-year, despite working capital rising by \$411 million (25%) due to higher accounts receivable and inventory from increased sales and input costs.**  
   Capital expenditures rose to \$310 million from \$218 million, driven primarily by \$254 million invested in the Southwest-Sinton Flat Roll Steel Division under construction. The company maintained strong liquidity with cash and equivalents of \$1.25 billion [10-Q 2021-04-29; 8-K 2021-04-20].

### Operations Insights

5. **Steel shipments were near-record at 2.8 million tons, down slightly (1-3%) from 2020Q1, but average steel selling prices increased 35% year-over-year to \$1,041 per ton, driving net sales growth in steel operations by 31%.**  
   Steel mill production was 2.48 million tons, slightly below 2.54 million tons in 2020Q1. Ferrous scrap cost per ton melted rose 39% to \$372, but selling prices increased more, expanding metal spread by 32% compared to 2020Q1 [8-K 2021-04-20; 10-Q 2021-04-29].

6. **Metals recycling shipments of ferrous scrap increased 17% year-over-year, with external shipments up 11%, benefiting from a 5% sequential increase in domestic steel mill utilization to 77%, which supported higher scrap prices and doubled operating income.**  
   Nonferrous shipments also increased 3%, supporting overall metals recycling revenue growth of 72% to \$1.08 billion [10-Q 2021-04-29].

7. **Steel fabrication shipments set a record at 184,000 tons, up 13% from 163,000 tons in 2020Q1, with net sales up 17% due to a 4% increase in average selling prices; however, operating income declined 66% due to a 24% increase in steel input costs outpacing selling price gains.**  
   The segment’s metal spread (difference between selling price and steel input cost) declined 19%, reflecting the timing mismatch of fixed backlog pricing against rising steel costs. Fabrication backlog was at a record high, 85% above prior peaks, indicating strong future demand [8-K 2021-04-20; 10-Q 2021-04-29].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

8. **Steel Dynamics benefited from strong domestic steel demand, particularly in automotive, construction, and industrial sectors, supported by historically low customer inventories and robust order entry across all business segments.**  
   The company highlighted record flat roll and strong long product steel selling values, with pricing gains across the entire steel platform. Steel joist and deck pricing also reached record levels due to demand and higher steel costs in fabrication [8-K 2021-04-20; 10-Q 2021-04-29].

### Market and Capacity Insights

9. **Construction of the Southwest-Sinton Flat Roll Steel Mill in Texas continued on schedule and within the \$1.9 billion budget, with steel production expected to begin late summer 2021.**  
   This new mill is designed to compete with integrated steel producers and foreign imports, offering broader product capabilities and lower carbon emissions. The company has secured co-location agreements with customers representing over 1.3 million tons of annual steel consumption and processing [8-K 2021-04-20].

10. **Steel Dynamics plans to invest \$175 million to \$200 million in two new flat roll steel coating lines in the U.S. Midwest, comprising a 300,000-ton galvanizing line with Galvalume® coating and a 240,000-ton paint line, expected to begin production in the second half of 2022.**  
    These investments aim to diversify value-added flat roll product offerings and enhance regional supply chain advantages [8-K 2021-04-19].

### Corporate and Risk Insights

11. **The company disclosed risks related to market and economic conditions, steel and recycled metals market fluctuations, and the operation of new and existing facilities, consistent with prior SEC filings.**  
    Forward-looking statements include uncertainties about global economies, steel demand, raw material costs, and trade policies. The company expects U.S. trade policies and existing steel trade cases to continue moderating steel imports [8-K 2021-04-19; 10-Q 2021-04-29].

### Wrap Up

Steel Dynamics delivered record financial and operating results in 2021Q1, driven by a sharp rise in steel prices amid strong demand from key end markets and historically low customer inventories. Steel operations and metals recycling segments posted substantial earnings gains, supported by expanded metal spreads and higher shipments, while steel fabrication earnings declined due to input cost pressures despite record shipments and backlog. The company continued significant capital investments, notably the near-complete Southwest-Sinton Flat Roll Steel Mill and planned Midwest coating lines, positioning for expanded product capabilities and regional market reach. Working capital growth reflected higher sales and raw material prices, with cash flow sufficient to support ongoing investments and maintain liquidity.

Management expressed confidence in continued momentum for 2021, citing strong domestic fundamentals and trade policy support, while acknowledging typical industry risks around market conditions and input costs. No operational disruptions or labor issues were disclosed for the quarter. The next major capacity addition is scheduled for late summer 2021 with the Southwest-Sinton mill start-up, and the new coating lines are targeted for second half 2022 production.

### Wrap Up

Steel Dynamics’ Q4 2023 results reflect a challenging steel pricing environment with metal spread compression reducing steel operations and fabrication profitability despite record shipments and steady volumes. The company’s diversified operations, including metals recycling and steel fabrication, faced sequential earnings declines due to pricing pressure and lower shipments, although order backlogs and recent price increases suggest some stabilization entering 2024. Year-to-date through September 30, 2024, the company invested \$1.4 billion in capital expenditures, paid \$212 million in dividends, and repurchased \$917 million of stock (4.5% of shares) [8-K 2024-10-17; 10-Q 2024-11-08; 8-K 2024-11-08].

### Operations Insights

4. **Steel operations shipments increased 3% to 3.2 million tons in 2024Q3 despite an 11% price decline, with production near prior year levels.**  
   Steel shipments totaled 3.2 million tons in 2024Q3, with 2.9 million tons excluding intra-segment transfers, a 3% increase over 2023Q3. Steel mill production was 2.79 million tons, essentially flat with 2023Q3. The average external steel selling price dropped 11% (\$130/ton), to \$1,059 per ton, while the average ferrous scrap cost per ton melted decreased 9% (\$38/ton) to \$367. Metal spread for steel operations contracted 12%, leading to a 37% operating income decline to \$301 million [10-Q 2024-11-08].

5. **Steel fabrication operations saw a 29% sales decline and a 50% operating income drop due to lower average selling prices and volume.**  
   Steel fabrication net sales declined 29% to \$450 million in 2024Q3, with average selling prices falling 28% (\$1,080/ton) and shipments down 2%. The metal spread contracted 36% due to the sharper price decline relative to steel input costs. Operating income dropped 50% to \$166 million from \$330 million in 2023Q3. Despite historically strong demand, pricing returned toward pre-pandemic levels [10-Q 2024-11-08].

6. **Metals recycling operating income fell 45% to \$7.7 million due to softer demand and an unexpected \$10 million copper hedging loss.**  
   Metals recycling shipments and pricing declined in 2024Q3 as many domestic steel mills had maintenance outages. An unrealized, non-cash copper hedging loss of \$10 million was recorded as copper prices rose sharply from August to September 2024. Operating income dropped to \$7.7 million from \$14.0 million in 2023Q3 [8-K 2024-10-17; 10-Q 2024-11-08].

7. **Aluminum operations segment reported an operating loss of \$23.6 million in 2024Q3, worsening from a \$7.2 million loss in 2023Q3.**  
   The aluminum segment, including the under-construction recycled aluminum flat rolled mill in Mississippi and slab centers in the US and Mexico, showed increased operating losses as construction and pre-operational costs rose. ### Commercial Strategy Insights

9. **Flat rolled steel sales, heavily contract-based (~80%), experienced lagging pricing tied to indices, driving price declines in 2024Q3.**  
   Approximately 80% of flat rolled steel sales are contractually tied to lagging pricing indices, causing realized average selling prices to decline 11% year-over-year despite stable demand. Pricing began stabilizing and improving late in 2024Q3, supported by low customer inventory and stable scrap prices [8-K 2024-10-17; 10-Q 2024-11-08].

    Four new value-added flat rolled steel coating lines began operating in early 2024, producing galvanized and painted products.     Construction continues on the aluminum flat rolled products mill in Columbus, Mississippi, and two recycled aluminum slab centers in the southwestern US and Mexico. The mill is a joint venture with Unity Aluminum, with Steel Dynamics holding a 94.4% stake. ### Corporate and Risk Insights

12. **The company disclosed no material litigation, labor disputes, or regulatory actions affecting financial condition or operations for 2024Q3.**  
    No material impacts from contract disputes, labor issues, or regulatory matters were reported for the quarter. The company referred to prior 10-K and 10-Q filings for detailed risk factors and forward-looking statements [10-Q 2024-11-08; 8-K 2024-10-17].

### Wrap Up

Steel Dynamics’ 2024 third quarter results reflect a challenging pricing environment with average steel selling prices down 11% year-over-year, driving a 46% drop in consolidated operating income to \$395 million despite stable or slightly higher steel shipment volumes. Metal spread compression across steel and fabrication segments was the primary margin driver, with steel operations’ operating income down 37% and steel fabrication’s down 50%. The metals recycling segment faced softer demand and a significant non-cash copper hedging loss, while aluminum operations deepened losses amid ongoing construction and pre-operational expenses.

Cash flow generation remained robust at \$760 million for the quarter, enabling substantial share repurchases and dividend payments while maintaining \$3.1 billion in liquidity. Commercially, Steel Dynamics is expanding higher-margin coated flat rolled steel capacity and advancing a new aluminum flat rolled mill targeting mid-2025 startup, aiming to diversify product offerings and end markets. The company reported no new material risks or operational interruptions affecting financial condition in the quarter.

**Guidance and Outlook:** Management expressed constructive views on 2025 steel market dynamics, anticipating steel price recovery driven by lower interest rates, onshoring trends, and public infrastructure funding. They expect benefits from trade actions limiting unfair imports, particularly for coated flat rolled steel, and foresee increased earnings contributions from new value-added coating lines in 2025. No specific quantitative guidance for 2025 was provided in the filings [8-K 2024-10-17].

    The March 13, 2020 acquisition of AK Steel added flat-rolled carbon, stainless, and electrical steel capabilities to Cleveland-Cliffs’ iron ore pellet business. It also issued \$725 million of 6.75% Senior Secured Notes on the acquisition date and \$955 million of 9.875% Senior Secured Notes in April 2020. These actions, alongside operational cost reductions and dividend suspension, were designed to maintain financial flexibility amid the pandemic [8-K 2020-04-02; 8-K 2020-04-15; 8-K 2020-04-17; 8-K 2020-04-24; 10-Q 2020-05-11].

### Wrap Up

Cleveland-Cliffs’ first quarter 2020 was dominated by the strategic acquisition of AK Steel, which transformed the company into a vertically integrated iron ore and steel producer. This drove a near doubling of revenues but also significant acquisition-related costs and amortization charges, resulting in a net loss of \$52.1 million. Operationally, mining production increased, and intercompany sales rose substantially, while the steel segment faced pandemic-induced demand drops and facility idlings, especially in the automotive sector. Cost controls, temporary labor pay cuts, and suspension of capital projects like the HBI plant were implemented to preserve liquidity.

To support financial stability amid COVID-19 disruptions, Cleveland-Cliffs raised substantial debt through new senior secured notes and amended its credit facilities, achieving approximately \$1.25 billion in liquidity by early May. The company’s product focus remains on high-quality, value-added steel and iron ore products with a leading automotive market share. However, management acknowledged ongoing demand uncertainty, particularly in automotive, and suspended prior guidance for 2020 due to the pandemic’s evolving impact. The company expects gradual production restarts aligned with market recovery timing.

### Wrap Up

Cleveland-Cliffs’ 2020 third quarter reflected a significant operational recovery from the severe disruptions earlier in the year caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, with revenues boosted by the March acquisition of AK Steel and improving product pricing, especially in flat-rolled steel. Despite a sharp rise in revenue to \$1.65 billion, net income contracted to \$2 million due to acquisition-related costs, idle expenses, and amortization charges. Operationally, shipments normalized by September, particularly in the automotive segment, while mining volumes remained depressed but rebounded as idled mines restarted. After acquisitions, fourth-quarter 2020 Adjusted EBITDA reached a six-year high of \$286 million, up from \$111 million in the prior-year quarter. However, full-year 2020 operating income was negative \$142 million versus positive \$429 million in 2019, reflecting acquisition costs and pandemic-related disruptions [8-K 2021-02-25; 10-K 2021-02-26].

3. **Cash Flow and Liquidity Maintained Despite Pandemic and Acquisitions**  
   The Company generated \$246 million in cash from operations in Q3 2020 and spent \$96 million on capital expenditures. Total liquidity as of October 19, 2020, was approximately \$1.2 billion, consisting of \$100 million in cash and \$1.1 billion available under its asset-based lending (ABL) facility. The Company repaid \$400 million in ABL borrowings over six months ending in Q3 2020 [8-K 2020-10-23; 8-K 2020-07-30]. Capital spending for 2020 was lowered to about \$500 million, including \$110 million remaining for the Toledo Hot Briquetted Iron (HBI) plant [8-K 2020-10-23].

4. **Debt Increased Significantly Post-Acquisitions with New Preferred Stock Issued**  
   Total liabilities increased from \$3.1 billion at year-end 2019 to \$13.7 billion at year-end 2020, reflecting debt assumed for acquisitions. Redeemable preferred stock of \$738 million was recorded at the end of 2020. Cliffs’ shareholders’ equity grew from \$358 million to \$2.3 billion, boosted by equity issuance tied to acquisitions [8-K 2021-02-25; 10-K 2021-02-26].

### Operations Insights

5. **Steel Production and Sales Volume Expanded Sharply with New Steelmaking Segment**  
   Following the acquisitions, Cliffs consolidated its segment reporting to one Steelmaking segment, which includes former Mining and Pelletizing. Steel product shipments in Q4 2020 were 1.9 million net tons, with full-year steel shipments of 3.8 million net tons. Average net selling price per ton of steel products was \$947 for the full year and \$880 in Q4 2020 [8-K 2021-02-25].

6. **Toledo HBI Plant Commissioning and Start-Up in Late 2020**  
   The state-of-the-art Direct Reduction plant in Toledo, Ohio, began operations in November 2020, with Hot Briquetted Iron (HBI) production starting in December 2020. The Company expects to ship HBI to third-party customers starting in Q1 2021 and reach full production by Q2 2021 [8-K 2021-01-25; 8-K 2021-02-25].

7. **COVID-19 Impacted Operations with Temporary Facility Idling and Demand Volatility**  
   Certain facilities and construction activities were temporarily idled during Q2 2020 due to the pandemic. The Company reported adjusted EBITDA losses of \$82 million in Q2 2020 but saw a return to normalized operating rates by Q3 2020, with positive adjusted EBITDA and improved shipment rates [8-K 2020-07-30; 8-K 2020-10-23].

8. **Raw Material Prices and Premiums Showed Mixed Trends Amid Pandemic**  
   Iron ore prices averaged \$89 per metric ton in Q1 2020, up 8% from the prior year, while the Atlantic Basin pellet premium declined 56% year-over-year but showed some recovery post-pandemic onset. Pellet premiums and iron ore prices remained relatively stable during the pandemic, supporting Cliffs’ pellet business [10-Q 2020-05-11; 10-Q 2020-07-30].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

9. **Transition to Vertically Integrated Producer with Emphasis on Value-Added Steel Products**  
   The acquisitions of AK Steel and ArcelorMittal USA transformed Cleveland-Cliffs into the largest flat-rolled steel producer in North America, integrating iron ore mining, pelletizing, steelmaking, and downstream manufacturing including tubing, tooling, and stamping. The Company targets differentiated, high-quality steel products primarily serving the automotive industry and infrastructure markets [8-K 2020-03-13; 8-K 2020-12-09; 10-K 2021-02-26].

10. **Pricing Environment and Product Mix Shift Toward Fixed-Price Contracts**  
    Management noted a shift from commodity-based pricing toward more fixed-price contracts with sophisticated steel products, which is expected to provide more predictable free cash flow. Average steel selling prices were \$947 per ton in 2020, reflecting a resilient pricing environment [8-K 2020-02-20; 8-K 2021-02-25].

### Market and Capacity Insights

11. **Acquisition of ArcelorMittal USA Expands Footprint and Capacity Significantly**  
    The December 2020 acquisition added six steelmaking facilities, eight finishing facilities, two iron ore mining and pelletizing operations, and three coal and cokemaking operations. This acquisition increased pro-forma 2019 revenues to approximately \$17 billion and adjusted EBITDA to \$1.7 billion, with expected annual cost synergies of about \$150 million [8-K 2020-12-09; 8-K 2020-09-28].

12. **Updated Segment Structure Reflects Integration of Mining and Steelmaking**  
    The former Mining and Pelletizing segment is now part of the Steelmaking segment, reflecting the integrated nature of iron ore pellets as primary raw materials for steel products. Other smaller segments such as Tooling and Stamping are classified as Other Businesses [8-K 2021-02-25].

### Corporate and Risk Insights

13. **Acquisition-Related Charges and Amortization Impact Earnings and Cash Flow**  
    The Company recorded acquisition-related costs of \$90 million in 2020, including amortization of inventory step-up of \$96 million. These non-cash and cash charges materially affected net income and operating income [8-K 2021-02-25].

14. **Exposure to Energy and Raw Material Supply Risks**  
    Cliffs discloses dependency on single sources for electric power and natural gas at many facilities, with potential material impact on production costs and margins if service or rates change significantly [10-K 2020-02-20].

15. **COVID-19 Pandemic Remains a Significant Operating Risk**  
    The Company acknowledges ongoing risks from COVID-19 disruptions to demand, supply chains, and operations, especially in key end markets like automotive. This uncertainty affected 2020 results and remains a factor in 2021 outlook [10-K 2021-02-26; 8-K 2020-05-11].

### Wrap Up

Cleveland-Cliffs’ 2020 fiscal year was marked by significant transformation through the acquisitions of AK Steel and ArcelorMittal USA, which expanded its operations from iron ore mining into fully integrated steelmaking and manufacturing. Revenues more than doubled to \$5.4 billion, but acquisition-related costs and pandemic disruptions led to a net loss of \$81 million. Adjusted EBITDA improved in the second half of the year, reaching \$286 million in Q4, supported by normalized operations and the commissioning of the Toledo HBI plant.

The Company shifted its segment reporting to reflect the integrated steelmaking business, combining mining and pelletizing with steel production. Pricing improved with a resilient steel market and a move toward fixed-price contracts, while raw material cost exposure remained a key factor. Liquidity remained solid through disciplined capital management and debt repayments despite increased leverage from acquisitions. COVID-19 continues to pose operational and market risks as Cliffs enters 2021 with a larger, more diversified footprint and ongoing capital investments.

**Guidance for 2021** includes capital expenditures of \$600-\$650 million, selling, general and administrative expenses of approximately \$450 million, depreciation and amortization around \$700 million, and interest expense near \$315 million in cash interest. The Company expects zero U.S. federal cash taxes and a non-cash effective income tax rate of about 20% [8-K 2021-02-25].

2021.Q1:
### Financial Insights

1. **Revenue and Earnings Increased Sharply Post-Acquisitions but Net Income Includes Significant Charges**  
Cleveland-Cliffs reported first-quarter 2021 consolidated revenues of \$4.0 billion, a massive increase from \$359 million in Q1 2020, largely reflecting the full-quarter inclusion of ArcelorMittal USA (AM USA) operations and AK Steel acquisition. Net income was \$41 million, or \$0.07 per diluted share, compared to a net loss of \$52 million in Q1 2020. Adjusted EBITDA rose dramatically to \$513 million from \$23 million a year earlier, with the Steelmaking segment contributing \$537 million of adjusted EBITDA, up from \$44 million. Cost of goods sold surged by \$3.4 billion to \$3.8 billion, reflecting the addition of about 3.9 million net tons of steel shipments from the acquisitions. Selling, general and administrative expenses increased by \$67 million to \$95 million, also driven by the expanded operational footprint. Acquisition-related costs were \$13 million in Q1 2021, down from \$42 million in Q1 2020, including \$11 million severance expenses [8-K 2021-04-22; 10-Q 2021-04-28].

3. **Cash Flow Impacted by Working Capital Build and Deferred Pension Contributions; Liquidity Remains Strong**  
Net cash used by operating activities was \$373 million in Q1 2021, compared to \$164 million used in Q1 2020. The working capital increase of approximately \$650 million was primarily due to unwinding the AM USA factoring agreement and rising receivables linked to higher steel prices. The company also made \$118 million in deferred pension contributions under the CARES Act during the quarter, which management noted will not recur. At April 19, 2021, total liquidity was approximately \$1.8 billion, supported by recent capital markets transactions and equity issuance proceeds used to redeem higher-cost debt [8-K 2021-04-22; 10-Q 2021-04-28].

4. **Capital Markets Activity Focused on Debt Refinancing and Extending Maturities**  
During Q1 2021, Cleveland-Cliffs issued \$500 million of 4.625% Senior Notes due 2029 and \$500 million of 4.875% Senior Notes due 2031, using proceeds to redeem all outstanding 4.875% 2024 Senior Secured Notes and 6.375% 2025 Senior Notes. Additionally, the company issued 20 million common shares for net proceeds of \$322 million, which along with cash on hand was used to repurchase \$322 million aggregate principal of 9.875% 2025 Senior Secured Notes. These actions extended debt maturities, increased unsecured debt ratio, and reduced high-cost debt [10-Q 2021-04-28].

5. **Full-Year 2021 Adjusted EBITDA Guidance Raised to \$4 Billion Based on Strong Pricing and Contract Renewals**  
The company increased its full-year 2021 adjusted EBITDA guidance by \$500 million to approximately \$4.0 billion, based on better-than-expected contract renewals and an assumed U.S. hot-rolled coil (HRC) steel price averaging \$1,100 per net ton for the final nine months. Q2 adjusted EBITDA is expected at \$1.2 billion. Management emphasized that the strong pricing environment is not luck but driven by fundamentals [8-K 2021-04-22].

### Operations Insights

6. **Steel Production and Shipments Expanded Sharply with Full Quarter of Acquired Operations**  
Steel product shipments totaled 4.1 million net tons in Q1 2021, up from 0.2 million net tons in Q1 2020. The product mix included 33% coated steel, 28% hot-rolled, 18% cold-rolled, 7% plate, 4% stainless and electrical steel, and 10% other products including slabs and rail. Steelmaking revenues of \$3.9 billion comprised 33% automotive sales, 32% distributors and converters, 24% infrastructure and manufacturing, and 11% steel producers. The average net selling price per ton was \$900, down from \$980 in Q1 2020, reflecting a product mix shift with a lower contribution of higher-priced coated, stainless, and electrical steels due to the AM USA acquisition [8-K 2021-04-22; 10-Q 2021-04-28].

7. **Raw Steel Production and Iron Ore Pellets Output Increased; Some Facilities Temporarily Idled**  
For Q1 2021, Cleveland-Cliffs produced 4.8 million net tons of raw steel, 6.9 million long tons of iron ore products, and 0.7 million net tons of coke. The Columbus and Monessen facilities acquired from AM USA remained temporarily idled due to COVID-19 impacts but Columbus was expected to restart in Q2 2021. By contrast, Q1 2020 production was 0.3 million net tons of raw steel and 4.8 million long tons of iron ore pellets [10-Q 2021-04-28].

8. **Steel Cost of Goods Sold Includes Significant Depreciation and Inventory Step-Up Amortization**  
Steelmaking cost of goods sold in Q1 2021 included \$206 million of depreciation, depletion, and amortization, and \$81 million of inventory step-up amortization related to the AM USA acquisition. These non-cash costs reflect the accounting for acquired assets and affect gross margins but not immediate cash costs [8-K 2021-04-22].

9. **Raw Material and Energy Price Exposure Managed via Fixed-Price Agreements and Hedging**  
The company faces exposure to market prices for electricity, natural gas, ferrous and stainless steel scrap, chrome, coal, coke, nickel, and zinc. Cleveland-Cliffs manages these risks by negotiating fixed-price contracts for certain raw materials and using forward physical purchases and derivative hedges. Some customer contracts have fixed pricing, which increases exposure to raw material cost fluctuations. Multi-year supply agreements with minimum purchase quantities also affect input cost risk [10-Q 2021-04-28].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

10. **Product Mix Shift Toward Lower-Priced Steel Products Post-AM USA Acquisition**  
The first full quarter of AM USA ownership reduced the overall contribution of higher-priced coated, stainless, and electrical steel products, causing the average net selling price per ton to decline to \$900 from \$980 in Q1 2020. Despite the lower average price, the company benefited from a record-high HRC domestic index price averaging \$1,201 per net ton in Q1 2021, up 105% year over year, which supports revenue growth and profitability [8-K 2021-04-22; 10-Q 2021-04-28].

11. **Strong Sales to Automotive and Infrastructure Markets with Flexible Volume Redirects**  
Steelmaking sales were distributed with 33% to automotive, 32% to distributors and converters, 24% to infrastructure and manufacturing, and 11% to steel producers. The company noted supply chain disruptions and a semiconductor shortage affecting automotive production, but was able to redirect volumes to the spot market where demand and prices were strong. U.S. light vehicle sales increased 11% year-over-year in Q1 2021, with dealer inventories at multi-year lows [8-K 2021-04-22; 10-Q 2021-04-28].

### Labor Insights

12. **Severance Costs Related to Acquisitions Declined but Remain Material**  
Acquisition-related costs included \$11 million of severance expenses in Q1 2021, down from \$19 million in Q1 2020. These expenses relate to integrating acquired operations and workforce adjustments. No other labor contract or workforce changes were disclosed [8-K 2021-04-22; 10-Q 2021-04-28].

### Wrap Up

Cleveland-Cliffs’ Q1 2021 results reflect the full integration of its major 2020 acquisitions of AK Steel and ArcelorMittal USA, driving a nearly elevenfold increase in revenue and a swing from net loss to net income. Adjusted EBITDA rose sharply, supported by record-high domestic hot-rolled coil steel prices and expanded production and shipments. However, net income was tempered by substantial non-cash charges related to inventory step-up amortization and debt extinguishment costs. The company’s product mix shifted toward lower-priced steel products due to the inclusion of AM USA’s product lines, impacting average selling prices per ton despite the strong steel price environment.

Operating cash flow was negative in Q1, largely due to a \$650 million working capital build linked to receivables and factoring unwind, as well as a one-time deferred pension contribution under the CARES Act. Liquidity remained robust at \$1.8 billion, supported by capital markets activity that extended debt maturities and reduced high-cost debt. Management raised full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance to \$4 billion, based on conservative pricing assumptions and contract renewals, signaling confidence in the current steel market conditions. The company continues to manage raw material and energy cost risks through fixed-price contracts and hedging while navigating supply chain disruptions affecting key end markets like automotive.

No material labor disputes or operational interruptions were reported, though some acquired facilities remained temporarily idled due to COVID-19 impacts with planned restarts in Q2. The company also emphasized its commitment to environmental sustainability with a stated goal to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 25% from 2017 levels by 2030.

**Guidance Summary:**  
- Full-year 2021 adjusted EBITDA guidance increased to approximately \$4.0 billion, up \$500 million from prior guidance.  
- Q2 2021 adjusted EBITDA expected to be approximately \$1.2 billion.  
- Assumes U.S. HRC steel price averages \$1,100 per net ton for the last nine months of 2021 [8-K 2021-04-22].  

No other specific upcoming risks or events beyond ongoing integration and market volatility were disclosed in the filings.

### Wrap Up

Cleveland-Cliffs’ Q3 2022 results reflected a significant margin contraction driven by higher input costs, lower shipment volumes, and elevated maintenance expenses, despite modest gains in steel selling prices and improved automotive shipments. The company’s steelmaking costs rose due to lagged inventory effects and inflationary pressures, though management expects a meaningful cost decline in Q4 2022. Operationally, the indefinite idle of a blast furnace aligned capacity with demand and supported quality improvements for automotive customers. The company’s vertical integration and domestic raw material sourcing continue to provide cost stability amid global supply disruptions.

Financially, Cleveland-Cliffs maintained solid liquidity, reduced debt, and executed share repurchases, while the recent USW labor agreement materially reduced pension and OPEB liabilities, improving future cash flow requirements. Market risks from commodity price volatility persist, with the company managing exposure through contracts and hedges. For full-year 2022, management anticipates an average steel selling price near \$1,370 per net ton, reflecting contract resets and product mix adjustments.

**Guidance Overview:**  
Management’s outlook for Q4 2022 includes steelmaking unit operating costs expected to decline by at least \$80 per net ton from Q3 levels, driven by reduced maintenance, higher production volumes, and lower energy/raw material costs. The company’s full-year 2022 average selling price is projected at approximately \$1,370 per net ton, based on current futures pricing and contract resets effective October 1, 2022 [8-K 2022-10-25].

### Financial Insights

1. **Cleveland-Cliffs reported stable revenues with improved profitability and cash flow in 2023Q3 despite lower steel prices.**  
   Revenues for Q3 2023 were \$5.6 billion, nearly flat compared to \$5.7 billion in Q3 2022, reflecting a 1% decrease in steelmaking revenues primarily due to a \$157 per net ton drop in average steel selling price, partially offset by a 13% increase in steel shipments to 4.1 million net tons. Net income rose to \$275 million (\$0.52 diluted EPS) from \$165 million (\$0.29 diluted EPS) in Q3 2022, boosted by higher adjusted EBITDA of \$614 million versus \$463 million a year earlier. Operating cash flow increased to \$767 million, supporting free cash flow of \$605 million, more than double the \$288 million in Q3 2022. The company used this cash primarily to reduce net debt by over \$500 million to \$3.4 billion and repurchased 3.9 million shares at an average price of \$15.09. Total liquidity reached a record \$4.4 billion [8-K 2023-10-23; 10-Q 2023-10-25].

2. **Steel unit costs fell substantially, with management targeting further reductions.**  
   Compared to Q3 2022, unit steel costs declined by \$165 per net ton. The company expects an additional \$15 per net ton cost reduction from Q3 to Q4 2023 and further decreases into 2024, including a \$250 million cost reduction locked in for metallurgical coal purchases. These cost improvements contributed to gross margin expansion to \$473 million in Q3 2023 from \$344 million in Q3 2022 despite lower average selling prices [\$165/unit cost decrease; 8-K 2023-10-23].

3. **Average steel selling prices declined, driven by weaker pricing in service center and steel producer markets, partially offset by automotive sector gains.**  
   The average selling price per net ton of steel products fell to \$1,203 in Q3 2023 from \$1,360 in Q3 2022, a 12% decrease. Revenues from distributors and converters declined 10%, and steel producers’ revenues fell 13%, mainly due to lower hot-rolled coil (HRC) and slab pricing indices. Conversely, direct automotive market revenues increased 13% to \$1.96 billion due to higher shipments and favorable fixed-price contract renewals. The automotive sector accounted for 36% of steel shipments and 36% of steelmaking revenues in Q3 2023 [10-Q 2023-10-25; 8-K 2023-10-23].

4. **The company’s diversified customer mix and contract structure moderated price volatility.**  
   Approximately 45% of volumes are sold under fixed-price contracts, which increased in value in 2023 compared to 2022, reducing exposure to spot price fluctuations. Index-linked contracts also contributed to stable revenue streams. This pricing mix helped offset the impact of volatile spot market prices, particularly in HRC, which averaged \$792 per net ton in Q3 2023, 5% below Q3 2022 but above the prior ten-year average [10-Q 2023-10-25].

### Operations Insights

5. **Steel shipments increased 13%, supported by record automotive shipments amid uneven service center demand due to the UAW strike.**  
   Steel shipments rose to 4.1 million net tons in Q3 2023 from 3.6 million in Q3 2022. Hot-rolled steel shipments surged 40% to 1.475 million net tons, driven by automotive demand. However, service centers purchased steel at very low volumes during Q3, prioritizing internal transactions amid the UAW strike affecting three Detroit-based automotive clients. Other major automotive clients outside Detroit compensated by increasing purchases, sustaining overall automotive steel shipments at record levels [8-K 2023-10-23; 10-Q 2023-10-25].

6. **Product mix shifted toward higher-value automotive steel and hot-rolled steel.**  
   The shipment mix in Q3 2023 was 36% hot-rolled, 30% coated, 14% cold-rolled, 6% plate, 4% stainless and electrical steel, and 10% other products including slabs and rail. The automotive market represented 36% of steel shipments and revenues, infrastructure and manufacturing 26%, distributors and converters 24%, and steel producers 14%. The higher-value automotive steel mix contributed to better-than-expected realized prices despite overall market softness [8-K 2023-10-23].

7. **Steel production efficiency improved with strategic use of direct reduced iron (DRI) and scrap, supporting lower coke consumption and carbon emissions.**  
   The company’s vertically integrated operations include iron ore pellets, direct reduced iron (DRI), and ferrous scrap. The Toledo DRI plant, with 1.9 million metric tons annual capacity, supports blast furnaces by enhancing productivity and reducing coke dependency. This integration allows Cleveland-Cliffs to maintain steel output with one less blast furnace since early 2022, improving operating efficiency and lowering carbon intensity [10-Q 2023-10-25].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

8. **Automotive steel shipments reached a new record, driven by easing supply chain constraints and light vehicle production recovery.**  
   The automotive industry experienced its highest light vehicle production through nine months of 2023 since 2019. Cliffs is the largest North American supplier to this sector and benefited from increased demand and favorable fixed-price contract renewals. Despite the UAW strike, shipments remained strong as other clients increased purchases. The company expects normalized service center buying patterns post-strike to further support demand in Q4 2023 and into 2024 [8-K 2023-10-23; 10-Q 2023-10-25].

9. **Service center demand was suppressed in Q3 due to strike anticipation but is expected to normalize in Q4.**  
   Service centers held significantly depleted inventories (1.6 months vs. a 10-year average of 2.2 months) and reduced purchases during the UAW strike period, impacting volumes. Management anticipates a return to normal buying behavior once the strike ends, which should support shipments and pricing going forward [8-K 2023-10-23; 10-Q 2023-10-25].

### Market and Capacity Insights

10. **Capacity expansions and product diversification continue, including electrical steel capacity and HBI production.**  
    The company commissioned an expansion of its NOES electrical steel capacity at the Zanesville facility, adding approximately 70,000 net tons annually. It is also the only producer of hot briquetted iron (HBI) in the Great Lakes region, produced at the Toledo direct reduction plant. HBI serves as a premium scrap alternative and productivity enhancer in blast furnaces and basic oxygen furnaces (BOFs), supporting margin improvement and carbon emission reduction [10-Q 2023-10-25].

11. **Long-term mineral leases secured for iron ore mining extend resource life and reduce supply uncertainty.**  
    In Q2 2023, Cliffs entered into long-term state mineral leases covering more than 2,600 acres at the Nashwauk mine site in Minnesota, resolving prior uncertainty about mine life. This supports the company’s vertically integrated raw material sourcing strategy [10-Q 2023-10-25].

### Corporate and Risk Insights

12. **Raw material and energy purchasing strategies mitigate price volatility but some exposure remains.**  
    The company uses annual and multi-year fixed-price agreements for key raw materials such as coal, coke, chrome, and industrial gases, and enters derivative contracts to hedge energy and material cost risks. Some customer contracts are fixed-price, increasing exposure to input cost fluctuations, though the company strives to align contract terms to reduce this risk. Minimum purchase quantities in supply agreements and multi-year transportation contracts also factor into risk management. Despite these measures, market price fluctuations for natural gas, electricity, scrap, and metallurgical coal remain a source of risk [10-Q 2023-10-25].

13. **Trade actions on tin mill products from China, Canada, and Germany may affect supply and pricing.**  
    The U.S. Commerce Department imposed preliminary antidumping duties ranging from 5.29% to 111.98% on certain tin and chromium-coated sheet steel imports from these countries. While the direct impact on Cliffs is not detailed, these tariffs reflect ongoing trade policy risks in steel markets [10-Q 2023-10-25].

### Wrap Up

Cleveland-Cliffs’ third quarter of 2023 demonstrated stable revenues and improved profitability driven by record automotive steel shipments and significant cost reductions, despite lower average steel prices and subdued service center demand amid the UAW strike. The company’s vertically integrated production and diversified contract portfolio helped mitigate pricing volatility. Strong operating cash flow enabled meaningful debt reduction and share repurchases, resulting in record liquidity and a leaner balance sheet. Capacity expansions in electrical steel and HBI production support ongoing margin and carbon intensity improvements. Raw material procurement strategies reduce but do not eliminate exposure to commodity price risks, while trade actions on imports add to market uncertainties.

Management expects further steel unit cost reductions in Q4 and 2024, normalization of service center buying post-strike, and continued free cash flow benefits from working capital improvements. Capital expenditure guidance for full-year 2023 was lowered to \$670 million from a prior midpoint of \$700 million. The company did not disclose specific next material events beyond the anticipated end of the UAW strike and ongoing cost reduction initiatives.

Cleveland-Cliffs’ 2024 results reflect a challenging steel market environment marked by sharply lower steel prices, reduced shipments, and weak automotive demand, leading to significant losses and negative adjusted EBITDA, especially in Q4. Cleveland-Cliffs’ 2025Q4 and full-year results reflect a steel industry environment marked by weak automotive demand, pricing pressures, and operational adjustments. The company took deliberate steps to optimize capacity, including idling mines and facilities, and focused its commercial strategy on securing multi-year automotive contracts and exploring strategic partnerships such as the MoU with POSCO. Liquidity remained strong despite negative operating cash flow, supported by financing activities and disciplined capital spending. Risks include exposure to commodity price volatility, foreign exchange fluctuations, and the long-term obligations embedded in raw material supply contracts. The company’s 2026 guidance anticipates modest shipment growth, further unit cost reductions, and increased capital expenditures focused on sustaining operations.

### Wrap Up

In 2025, Cleveland-Cliffs experienced a significant financial setback, with a GAAP net loss doubling to \$1.43 billion and adjusted EBITDA collapsing to \$37 million. This deterioration was driven by weak automotive demand, an adverse slab contract, and Canadian market challenges, despite a modest increase in steel shipments and a shift toward higher-margin hot-rolled and plate products. The company actively optimized its footprint by idling and permanently closing underperforming facilities while maintaining strong liquidity above \$3 billion and reducing capital expenditures to conserve cash.

Strategically, Cleveland-Cliffs expanded its geographic and product footprint through the Stelco acquisition and advanced a partnership with POSCO to leverage its U.S. operations. Operationally, raw material and energy costs were managed effectively to reduce unit costs by approximately \$50 per net ton in 2025 versus 2024. The company also faces ongoing risks from commodity price volatility, labor market challenges, and regulatory factors. Debt maturities were extended, and share repurchases were modest during the year.

**Guidance for 2026** includes steel shipments of approximately 16.5–17.0 million net tons, further unit cost reductions of about \$10 per net ton, capital expenditures around \$700 million, selling, general and administrative expenses near \$575 million, depreciation of about \$1.1 billion, and pension and OPEB contributions of approximately \$125 million [10-K filed 2026-02-09]. No material operational interruptions or labor disputes were disclosed for 2025. The company’s focus remains on cost discipline, footprint optimization, and leveraging strategic partnerships to improve performance in 2026.

Inventory levels increased slightly by \$229 million, partially offsetting cash outflows. Non-cash charges such as depreciation and pension credits also affected operating cash flow. The company returned to positive free cash flow in Q2 after prior quarters of cash burn, enabling initial debt reduction. [8-K 2026-07-23; 10-Q 2026-07-23]

### Operations Insights

6. **Steel product shipment volumes declined 6% year-over-year in Q2 2026, with notable decreases in slab and plate shipments but growth in hot-rolled and coated steel volumes.**  
   Hot-rolled steel shipments grew 6% to 1.82 million net tons, coated steel rose 9% to 1.24 million net tons, and stainless and electrical steel shipments increased 18% to 159 thousand net tons. Conversely, plate shipments fell 21% to 172 thousand net tons, and slab and other steel product shipments declined sharply by 96% to 16 thousand net tons as the company concluded its unprofitable semi-finished steel slab contract in December 2025. The overall decline in shipments reflects a strategic shift away from lower-margin slab sales toward higher-value flat-rolled steel products. [10-Q 2026-07-23]

7. **The company continued to optimize its integrated steelmaking footprint by idling or permanently closing underperforming facilities and consolidating plate production to improve utilization and cost efficiency.**  
   In Q2 2026, Cleveland-Cliffs idled the Gary plate finishing line and one of two plate mills at Burns Harbor, consolidating all plate production at a single Burns Harbor mill. Earlier decisions included idling the blast furnace, basic oxygen furnace (BOF) steel shop, and continuous casting at Dearborn, and permanently closing the Steelton, Conshohocken, and Riverdale facilities. The Minorca mine was idled and the Hibbing mine partially idled. These moves aimed to streamline operations and enhance efficiency without reducing flat-rolled steel output. [10-Q 2026-07-23]

8. **Routine maintenance outages in April and May 2026 temporarily impacted steel unit costs and production efficiency.**  
   The timing of these outages contributed to elevated steel unit costs in Q2 2026, alongside a product mix shift and higher diesel fuel prices. Management indicated that despite these outages, operational results improved from Q1. [8-K 2026-07-23; 10-Q 2026-07-23]

### Commercial Strategy Insights

9. **The company’s product mix shifted toward higher-margin hot-rolled steel following the end of a semi-finished slab supply contract in December 2025, improving overall revenue quality.**  
   The slab contract, which represented approximately 10% of sales volume and was unprofitable in 2025, concluded in Q1 2026. This allowed Cleveland-Cliffs to increase sales of value-added flat-rolled products such as hot-rolled and coated steel, which commanded higher average selling prices and margins. The commercial strategy emphasizes increasing throughput on coating assets, historically underutilized, to better align product mix with customer demand and fixed-cost absorption. [10-Q 2026-07-23]

10. **Sales to key markets showed growth in automotive and distributor channels, while infrastructure and steel producer sales declined slightly.**  
    Q2 2026 steelmaking revenues by market were \$1.46 billion (up 17%) to automotive, \$1.64 billion (up 14%) to distributors and converters, \$1.43 billion (down 4%) to infrastructure and manufacturing, and \$526 million (down 12%) to steel producers. The automotive market remains the largest end-use, supported by stable North American light vehicle production (~3.9 million units in Q2 2026). [10-Q 2026-07-23]

11. **The Canadian steel market showed signs of recovery with lower than historical import levels and improved margins at Stelco, supported by Canadian tariff-rate quotas.**  
    Management highlighted the importance of protecting the Canadian steel industry to preserve economic and national security interests. Stelco's position is improving, contributing to the company’s expectation of a return to significant earnings from this segment. [8-K 2026-07-23; 10-Q 2026-07-23]

12. **A Memorandum of Understanding with POSCO reflects potential strategic partnership opportunities to leverage Cleveland-Cliffs’ U.S. footprint and trade-compliant operations.**  
    POSCO, a major South Korean steel producer, aims to support and grow its U.S. customer base by collaborating with Cleveland-Cliffs. This partnership remains subject to negotiation and formal agreements but could enhance Cleveland-Cliffs’ commercial reach and product offerings. UBS is acting as financial advisor for this potential transaction. [10-Q 2026-07-23]

### Wrap Up

In Q2 2026, Cleveland-Cliffs demonstrated a significant operational and financial turnaround compared to Q1 by tripling adjusted EBITDA to \$286 million and returning to positive operating cash flow of \$230 million. This improvement was driven by higher steel prices, a shift in product mix toward higher-margin flat-rolled steel, and ongoing footprint optimization, including idling underperforming facilities and consolidating plate production. Despite a 6% decline in steel shipments, revenue grew 6% year-over-year due to pricing and mix gains. The company maintained strong liquidity at \$3.1 billion and affirmed full-year shipment and capital expenditure guidance.

Commercially, the company benefited from increased sales to automotive and distributor markets and a recovering Canadian steel market supported by trade protections. A strategic partnership with POSCO is under negotiation, reflecting management’s intent to leverage Cleveland-Cliffs’ U.S. platform. Elevated diesel costs and maintenance outages constrained unit cost improvements, but overall margin and cash flow trends were positive. The Q3 2026 adjusted EBITDA outlook of approximately \$575 million indicates management’s expectation of continued operational leverage.

No material new risks or labor developments were disclosed for the quarter. The company's ongoing strategic focus remains on optimizing its integrated steelmaking footprint, improving utilization of coating assets, and aligning product mix with higher-value applications to enhance fixed-cost absorption and margin performance.

### Wrap Up

In Q3 2020, Commercial Metals Company experienced a notable earnings and sales contraction driven by lower steel prices and shipment volumes across its segments, largely reflecting the economic disruptions from COVID-19. The Americas Mills segment faced margin compression but improved conversion costs sequentially, while the Americas Fabrication segment achieved its best quarterly profitability in nearly 12 years, supported by strong backlog and pricing. Americas Recycling and International Mill segments were more adversely affected by weak demand and pricing declines. The company maintained strong cash flow and liquidity, enabling continued dividend payments and network optimization, including facility closures.

Looking ahead, CMC highlighted resilient construction activity and a robust fabrication backlog as supportive factors for near-term volumes. The company’s risk management includes commodity and currency hedging to mitigate input cost volatility. However, the ongoing pandemic's broader financial effects remain uncertain. No specific guidance was disclosed for periods beyond Q3 2020 in the filings reviewed.

### Wrap Up

In fiscal 2020, Commercial Metals Company demonstrated improved earnings and cash flow generation despite COVID-19 headwinds and raw material cost pressures. Sequential quarterly gains in adjusted earnings and core EBITDA reflected disciplined cost management and resilience in shipments supported by strong fabrication backlogs. The strategic announcement of a third micro mill in Arizona signals continued investment in innovative, higher-margin product capacity aligned with market demand in the U.S. West Coast. Vertical integration remains central to operating efficiency, while trade and import pressures, particularly in Europe, continue to weigh on steel product margins over scrap cost. The company’s balance sheet strengthened significantly with increased cash and reduced debt, supporting ongoing capital projects and a steady dividend policy.

One-time charges related to acquisition settlements and facility closures affected reported earnings but are excluded from adjusted results. ### Financial Insights

Europe’s segment adjusted EBITDA improved from \$11.4 million to \$14.5 million due to volume growth and cost reductions, despite an \$18/ton margin decline over scrap. ### Operations Insights
