   Total finished steel shipments in North America were flat year-over-year at 750,000 tons, with a 2% increase in mill-produced rebar volumes (486,000 tons) supported by construction activity resilience. Merchant and other product shipments grew 12% (264,000 tons vs. 236,000 tons prior year), reflecting strategic focus on this segment through expanded product offerings and service capabilities. Downstream product shipments declined 42,000 tons due to backlog contraction and Gulf Coast weather disruptions. European shipments of steel products rose 17% to 397,000 tons, driven by increased industrial activity and construction demand in Poland and Central Europe [8-K 2021-01-11; 10-Q 2021-01-11].

   North America achieved its lowest mill conversion cost per ton since before the fiscal 2019 rebar asset acquisition, reflecting strong cost management.    Ferrous scrap costs in North America increased \$40 per ton year-over-year to \$266 per ton, while steel product average selling prices declined \$14 per ton, compressing metal margins from \$400 to \$346 per ton. In Europe, scrap costs rose \$18 per ton to \$262, with steel product prices flat at \$461 per ton, reducing metal margin per ton from \$217 to \$199.    CMC’s strategic growth initiatives include expanding merchant and other product shipments, which increased 12% in North America. Residential construction and industrial activity trends in North America and Europe were cited as positive demand indicators for merchant products. The company is actively adjusting pricing on rebar and merchant mill products to respond to rising scrap costs, though margin headwinds are expected to persist into the next quarter due to price lag [8-K 2021-01-11].

   CMC incurred \$5.9 million in net after-tax charges related to facility closure expenses and asset impairments primarily from decommissioning Steel California operations. This closure is part of ongoing efforts to optimize the production network and is expected to yield cost benefits in future periods. The Rancho Cucamonga melting operations were closed in October 2019, with production ceasing in December 2020, and the site is planned for sale [8-K 2021-01-11; 10-Q 2021-01-11].

10. **European facility capacity supported by new rolling line startup and industrial demand**  
    The Europe segment’s shipment volumes increased 17% year-over-year, driven by rebar shipments supported by a resilient Polish construction sector and merchant bar and wire rod shipments benefiting from Central European manufacturing activity. The company noted the startup of a third Polish rolling line on schedule, contributing to capacity expansion [8-K 2021-01-11].

### Corporate and Risk Insights

11. **Commodity derivatives resulted in increased losses reflecting market volatility**  
    Commodity derivatives not designated as hedges caused pre-tax losses of \$5.6 million in Q1 FY2021, compared to \$1.3 million in the prior year period, recorded within cost of goods sold. Cash flow hedging instruments produced a net gain of \$1.2 million. The company uses derivatives to hedge exposure to raw materials and energy costs, including copper and electricity, but some contracts are not designated for hedge accounting despite being economic hedges [10-Q 2021-01-11].

### Wrap Up

CMC’s first quarter of fiscal 2021 reflected the continuing impact of elevated ferrous scrap costs and COVID-19 related demand uncertainty, which compressed steel and downstream product margins despite stable shipments and strong cost control. The company’s operational focus on controlling costs led to mill conversion costs at two-year lows, partially offsetting raw material price pressure. Strategic growth in merchant bar and wire rod shipments contributed to volume resilience, supported by a solid construction backlog in North America and industrial activity in Europe.

Financially, CMC maintained a strong liquidity position with \$465 million cash and robust credit availability, enabling continued capital investments in micro mill expansions and rolling line startups. Closure of Steel California operations advanced network optimization but added near-term charges. Management signaled persistent margin headwinds due to scrap cost volatility and a lag in price adjustments, with expectations of typical seasonal shipment patterns in the next quarter.

No specific forward-looking financial guidance was disclosed in the filings beyond the fiscal 2021 capital expenditure range of \$200 million to \$225 million and the expectation of ongoing margin pressure in the near term. The company’s risk disclosures highlight commodity price volatility and derivative-related losses as ongoing considerations.

   North America segment net sales increased to \$1.66 billion in Q4 2021 from \$1.22 billion a year earlier. Adjusted EBITDA rose 22% to \$212.0 million from \$174.2 million. Finished steel shipments (steel products plus downstream) increased 2% year-over-year, with a 29% increase in merchant and other product shipments offsetting a modest decline in rebar shipments due to mix shift toward merchant bar and wire rod. Steel product margins over ferrous scrap increased by \$103 per ton compared to the prior year and \$41 per ton sequentially, reaching \$315 per ton in Q4 2021. However, controllable costs per ton increased year-over-year due to inflationary pressures in freight, labor, and mill consumables, partially offsetting margin gains [8-K 2021-10-14].

   The Europe segment reported record adjusted EBITDA of \$67.7 million in Q4 2021, up 195% from \$22.9 million a year earlier. Finished steel shipments in Europe increased to 460,000 tons in Q4 2021 from 380,000 tons in Q4 2020. The successful commissioning and ramp-up of the third rolling line in Poland contributed meaningfully to these results [8-K 2021-10-14].

   As of August 31, 2021, CMC held \$497.7 million in cash and cash equivalents with \$668.2 million available under credit and accounts receivable facilities, reflecting a strong liquidity position.    CMC reported a \$25 million annual EBITDA benefit from network optimization activities and achieved a year-over-year reduction in North America controllable costs per ton for six consecutive quarters through Q3 2021.    Average selling prices for steel products increased by approximately \$300 per ton year-over-year in Q4 2021 and \$170 per ton in Q3 2021 compared to the prior year quarters.     While rebar shipments declined modestly in Q4 2021 compared to prior year, shipments of merchant and other products increased substantially (29% year-over-year). This shift in product mix toward merchant bar and wire rod, typically higher-margin products, contributed to overall margin expansion despite lower rebar volumes. Europe also saw shipment growth in rebar (+16%) and merchant and other products (+24%) [8-K 2021-10-14].

### Corporate and Risk Insights

11. **No Material Operational Interruptions or Litigation Disclosed; Focus on Sustainability and Environmental Goals**  
    The filings did not disclose any major operational interruptions, labor disputes, or material litigation affecting CMC during fiscal 2021. These sustainability initiatives align with CMC’s long-standing business model based on recycling and energy efficiency [10-K 2021-10-14; 8-K 2021-10-14].

   Despite lower shipment volumes, average selling prices for steel products increased by \$346 per ton year-over-year, while ferrous scrap costs rose by \$92 per ton, resulting in a \$254 per ton expansion in steel product margin over scrap [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   Downstream product average selling prices rose nearly \$240 per ton year-over-year and \$77 per ton sequentially, reflecting ongoing backlog repricing [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   Controllable costs per ton increased sequentially due to maintenance, freight, and alloys [8-K 2022-03-17].  

4. **North America Segment Delivered Record Adjusted EBITDA on Margin Expansion Despite Lower Shipments**  
   North America segment adjusted EBITDA was \$535.5 million in Q2 FY22, including the real estate gain; excluding it, adjusted EBITDA was \$262.1 million, up 53% from \$171.6 million in Q2 FY21 [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   The segment’s steel product shipments declined from 740,000 tons in Q2 FY21 to 652,000 tons in Q2 FY22, and downstream shipments increased slightly to 327,000 tons from 343,000 tons a year ago [10-Q 2022-03-23].  
   Steel product metal margin per ton in North America increased by \$254 year-over-year, while raw material sales margins expanded for eight consecutive quarters [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   Adjusted EBITDA per ton of finished steel shipped in North America increased to \$268 in Q2 FY22, up from \$158 in Q2 FY21 [8-K 2022-03-17].

5. **Europe Segment Achieved Record Adjusted EBITDA on Margin Expansion and Production Capacity Utilization**  
   Europe segment adjusted EBITDA reached a record \$81.1 million in Q2 FY22, a 404% increase from \$16.1 million in Q2 FY21 [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   This was driven by a \$203 per ton year-over-year increase in margin over scrap and the addition of CMC Poland’s third rolling line, which improved production flexibility and allowed increased shipments of rebar, merchant bar, and wire rod [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   Finished steel shipments in Europe rose to 450,000 tons in Q2 FY22 from 353,000 tons in Q2 FY21 [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   Energy costs increased year-over-year but were more than offset by hedging and market factors; notably, Polish electricity rates were less volatile than Western Europe [8-K 2022-03-17].

6. **Raw Material and Energy Costs Increased but Were Offset by Pricing and Hedging**  
   Cost of ferrous scrap utilized per ton increased by \$92 year-over-year to \$444 per ton in North America and by a similar magnitude in Europe [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   Energy costs rose in Europe but were mitigated by a hedged position and relatively stable local electricity rates [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   The spread of selling price over purchase cost for raw materials expanded by \$52 per ton year-over-year, supporting margin growth [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   Controllable costs per ton increased sequentially due to maintenance, freight, and alloys expenses [8-K 2022-03-17].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

7. **Backlog Growth and Pricing Momentum Support Demand Outlook and Margin Sustainability**  
   North America downstream backlog grew 9% year-over-year for the third consecutive quarter, with new project bid volumes reaching record levels in Q2 FY22, indicating a robust construction project pipeline [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   Average selling prices for downstream products increased \$77 per ton sequentially, reflecting ongoing repricing of backlog contracts driven by higher-priced new awards [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   Management expects continued strong demand and margin levels through the spring and summer construction season, with Q3 FY22 shipments anticipated to increase seasonally and margins to remain at high levels [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   Europe volumes are expected to remain supported by a robust residential construction market and growth in industrial activity [8-K 2022-03-17].

8. **Growth Strategy Advancing with Acquisition and Facility Expansion**  
   CMC is progressing on its growth strategy, including the pending acquisition of Tensar Corporation, expected to close in fiscal Q3 2022, which will extend CMC’s presence in engineered solutions for construction reinforcement [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   The Arizona 2 micro mill project remains on schedule for early calendar 2023 startup; it is the first merchant bar-capable micro mill globally and will replace higher-cost rebar production from the former Steel CA plant [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   A fourth micro mill in the Eastern U.S. is planned, with site selection underway, aiming to enhance production flexibility, customer service, and logistics [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   These expansions leverage existing excess melt capacity and are expected to improve operational efficiency and product mix [8-K 2022-03-17].

### Market and Capacity Insights

9. **Operational Capacity Utilization Impacted by Maintenance but Enhanced by New Rolling Line in Europe**  
   Production was reduced in Q2 FY22 due to scheduled routine maintenance in North America, contributing to the shipment decline year-over-year [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   In Europe, the new third rolling line in Poland is operating at high utilization, consuming previous excess billet melt capacity that was formerly sold externally, thereby increasing finished steel output and market responsiveness [8-K 2022-03-17].  
   This enhanced production flexibility in Poland supported increased shipments and contributed to margin expansion [8-K 2022-03-17].

### Corporate and Risk Insights

10. **Geopolitical Risks from Ukraine Conflict Monitored but No Operational Disruption to Date**  
    Management acknowledged the war in Ukraine as a significant geopolitical and economic risk but reported no disruptions to CMC’s operations, workforce, or end-market demand as of the end of Q2 FY22 [8-K 2022-03-17].  
    The crisis is expected to tighten supply of long steel products in Central and Eastern Europe, potentially affecting market dynamics [8-K 2022-03-17].  
    The company’s risk disclosures also highlight the cyclical nature of the steel industry, sensitivity to raw material price volatility, and potential impacts from COVID-19 and trade policies [8-K 2022-03-17].

### Wrap Up

For fiscal Q2 2022, Commercial Metals Company delivered record earnings driven by a substantial gain on the sale of Southern California real estate and significant margin expansion across its North America and Europe steel product segments. Despite a 10% decline in shipments largely due to maintenance and weather, pricing power and backlog growth supported robust margins and adjusted EBITDA gains. The company’s liquidity and capital structure improved with opportunistic debt financing and real estate proceeds, enabling continued investment in growth projects such as the Arizona 2 micro mill and the pending Tensar acquisition. While geopolitical risks from the Ukraine conflict are noted, operations and demand remained stable through the quarter.

Management’s outlook anticipates sustained strong demand and margin levels into fiscal Q3 2022, with shipments expected to follow typical seasonal increases. The company’s strategic focus on expanding capacity and product offerings through new micro mills and acquisitions aims to leverage its existing platform for long-term growth. No material operational disruptions or labor issues were disclosed, and cost pressures from raw materials and energy were largely offset by pricing and hedging strategies.

### Financial Insights

1. **Net earnings and Core EBITDA more than doubled year-over-year, reflecting strong pricing and margin expansion.**

Adjusted EBITDA for North America increased 83% to \$379.4 million, and Europe’s adjusted EBITDA rose 142% to \$121.0 million, both reflecting strong market conditions and pricing [8-K 2022-06-16; 10-Q 2022-06-22].

2. **Average selling prices increased substantially, outpacing rising input costs and supporting margin gains.**  
   Steel product average selling prices increased by \$316 per ton year-over-year in North America, while the cost of ferrous scrap utilized rose by \$103 per ton. The margin over scrap for steel products expanded by \$213 per ton. Similarly, downstream products’ average selling price grew by \$281 per ton year-over-year and \$75 sequentially. In Europe, steel product prices increased by \$303 per ton year-over-year with scrap costs rising \$154 per ton, resulting in a \$149 per ton margin expansion. These price increases outpaced inflationary pressures on freight, energy, and alloys [8-K 2022-06-16; 10-Q 2022-06-22].

3. **Shipments of finished steel remained stable year-over-year despite seasonal patterns and operational constraints.**

North America shipments were 1.178 million tons, up slightly from 1.197 million tons in the prior year but down sequentially from 1.429 million tons in Q2 FY22. Europe shipments increased to 476,000 tons from 404,000 tons year-over-year, supported by high utilization of a third rolling line in Poland [8-K 2022-06-16].

4. **Cash and liquidity remained strong despite \$550 million net cash outflow for the Tensar acquisition and share repurchases.**  
   Cash and cash equivalents were \$410.3 million at May 31, 2022, down from \$497.7 million at August 31, 2021, reflecting the \$550 million payment (net of cash acquired) for Tensar. Restricted cash increased to \$126.3 million from \$3.4 million, likely related to acquisition or project financing. Available credit and accounts receivable facilities totaled \$624.3 million. CMC repurchased approximately 1 million shares for \$38.6 million during the quarter, with \$294.4 million remaining under the \$350 million authorization. The company declared a quarterly dividend of \$0.14 per share, a 17% increase from the prior year dividend [8-K 2022-06-16].

5. **Goodwill and intangible assets increased sharply due to the Tensar acquisition, impacting balance sheet composition.**  
   Goodwill rose to \$253.6 million from \$66.1 million, and intangible assets increased to \$266.4 million from \$10.1 million as of May 31, 2022, reflecting the acquisition completed in late April 2022. Total assets increased to \$6.1 billion from \$4.6 billion at August 31, 2021 [8-K 2022-06-16].

### Operations Insights

6. **Operational flexibility and high utilization in Europe offset energy cost inflation and geopolitical challenges.**  
   The addition of a third rolling line in Poland enabled record shipments and earnings in Europe despite significant increases in electricity costs and market disruptions related to the war in Ukraine and sanctions on Russia and Belarus. Energy cost increases were largely offset by a hedged position and less volatile electricity rates in Poland compared to Western Europe. European steel product margin over scrap increased by \$149 per ton year-over-year [8-K 2022-06-16].

7. **North America controllable costs per ton were flat sequentially but increased year-over-year due to freight, energy, and alloy costs.**  
   Despite inflationary pressures on freight, energy, and alloys, controllable costs per ton of finished steel shipped in North America remained unchanged from Q2 FY22 but were higher than in Q3 FY21. Planned maintenance activities and constrained labor at some construction sites partially limited shipment growth [8-K 2022-06-16; 10-Q 2022-06-22].

8. **Steelmaking inputs costs rose but were mitigated by price increases and energy derivative gains.**  
   The cost of ferrous scrap utilized increased 41% year-over-year in Q3 FY22. However, gains from energy derivatives designated as cash flow hedges totaled \$4.8 million in the quarter, compared to immaterial gains in the prior year period. Additionally, a \$15.5 million energy credit was received in Q1 FY22, reducing cost of goods sold [10-Q 2022-06-22].

9. **Downstream backlog volume and pricing hit record levels, supporting near-term shipment stability.**  
   CMC reported record bid activity and backlog levels on both volume and price bases in North America downstream products for the fourth consecutive quarter. Future pricing indicators remain positive, with new contract bid levels climbing significantly year-over-year. This backlog underpins expectations for stable volumes in Q4 FY22 [8-K 2022-06-16].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

10. **The Tensar acquisition diversifies CMC’s product portfolio and adds a new growth platform with high margin and low capital intensity.**  
    Completed in late April 2022, Tensar contributed EBITDA of \$4.9 million in its first five weeks, with \$7.1 million EBITDA excluding a \$2.2 million purchase accounting inventory charge, on net sales of \$28 million. Tensar’s EBITDA margin of 25.4% aligns with its five-year average. The acquisition extends CMC’s market reach into geogrids and foundation systems, enhances infrastructure exposure, and is expected to generate commercial synergies leveraging CMC’s sales culture and operational excellence [8-K 2022-06-16].

11. **Pricing and product mix improvements drove sustained margin expansion across steel products, raw materials, and downstream products.**  
    Steel products experienced five consecutive quarters of year-over-year margin expansion, while raw material sales margins grew for nine consecutive quarters. Margins on downstream products were above long-term averages, reflecting full value chain profitability. The spread of selling price over purchase cost for raw materials increased by \$47 per ton year-over-year in North America [8-K 2022-06-16].

12. **Market conditions and structural trends support a positive outlook for construction-related steel demand.**  
    CMC cited several structural trends underpinning demand, including strong single-family housing construction since early 2020, federal infrastructure funding increases (65% more for surface transportation), reshoring of critical industries adding about 500,000 tons of low-cost production, and a 14-year high in commercial and institutional non-residential construction starts. These factors are expected to support continued strength and backlog growth in fiscal 2023 [8-K 2022-06-16].

### Market and Capacity Insights

13. **Operational expansion with Arizona 2 micro mill startup planned for early calendar 2023 to enhance production flexibility.**  
    The Arizona 2 micro mill, expected to start in early 2023, will add about 1.5 million tons of incremental annual rebar capacity and provide flexibility to shift production between rebar and merchant bar products. This expansion aligns with rising demand and reshoring trends [8-K 2022-06-16].

### Corporate and Risk Insights

14. **Geopolitical events and import sanctions on Russia and Belarus expected to tighten supply and support European steel product margins.**  
    Import sanctions against Russia and Belarus are anticipated to reduce long steel product supply in Central and Eastern Europe, creating favorable market conditions for CMC Europe. The company highlighted these sanctions as a factor in its expectation for continued margin strength in Europe [8-K 2022-06-16].

15. **CMC maintains a disciplined capital allocation strategy balancing growth, shareholder returns, and debt management.**  
    The company’s priorities include funding growth initiatives such as the Arizona 2 project (partially financed by a tax-exempt bond), completing the Tensar acquisition, share repurchases, dividend payments, and opportunistic debt redemption. As of Q3 FY22, \$294.4 million remained authorized for share repurchases, and the dividend was increased 17% year-over-year [8-K 2022-06-16].

### Wrap Up

In Q3 FY22, Commercial Metals Company delivered substantially higher earnings driven by strong steel product pricing and margin expansion that outpaced rising scrap and input costs. Shipments remained stable amid some operational constraints, supported by record downstream backlog and pricing. The strategic acquisition of Tensar added a new, profitable growth platform with low capital intensity and broadened CMC’s product and geographic footprint. Operationally, Europe benefited from high utilization and hedging to offset energy cost inflation, while North America faced higher freight and alloy costs but maintained controllable cost discipline. Geopolitical factors and federal infrastructure funding underpin a positive demand outlook, with the Arizona 2 micro mill startup planned to enhance capacity flexibility in early 2023. CMC’s strong liquidity position supported acquisition funding, share repurchases, and dividend increases, reflecting a balanced capital allocation approach.

**Guidance:**  
CMC expects Q4 FY22 financial results to remain strong, with finished steel shipment volumes consistent with Q3 seasonal patterns and margins near Q3 levels across North America and Europe. The company anticipates continued robust demand and backlog growth driven by infrastructure spending, reshoring, and residential and non-residential construction trends entering fiscal 2023 [8-K 2022-06-16].

### Financial Insights

1. **Record Fiscal Year 2022 Earnings and Margins Supported by Higher Pricing and Operational Execution**  
Commercial Metals Company (CMC) reported fiscal fourth quarter 2022 net earnings of \$288.6 million, or \$2.40 per diluted share, an 89% increase from \$152.3 million, or \$1.24 per diluted share, in the prior year quarter. Excluding a \$6.5 million purchase accounting inventory charge, Tensar’s EBITDA was \$16.7 million on \$74.1 million of net sales, yielding a 22.5% margin. ### Operations Insights

4. **Finished Steel Shipments and Production Show Seasonal Patterns with Regional Variations**  
Total finished steel shipments in Q4 2022 were 1.132 million tons in North America (steel products only) and 428,000 tons in Europe. North America shipments declined slightly from 1.178 million tons in Q3 2022, consistent with typical seasonal patterns, and were down modestly from 1.186 million tons in Q4 2021, partly due to customer destocking and slower construction site activity related to labor shortages. Europe shipments rebounded late in Q4 after a supply chain destocking cycle earlier in the quarter, with volumes up sequentially but down year-over-year due to the prior quarter’s safety stock buildup.  
The commissioning of a third rolling mill line in Poland improved operational flexibility and allowed Europe segment to shift away from billet sales to finished product sales, enhancing margins. The Arizona 2 micro mill construction was on track for spring 2023 startup, expected to add approximately 500,000 tons of low-cost, flexible production capacity.

5. **Raw Material Costs and Energy Exposure Increased, Partially Offset by Operational and Hedging Measures**  
Cost of ferrous scrap utilized per ton in North America averaged \$435 in Q4 2022, down \$47 per ton from Q4 2021’s \$482 but up sequentially from \$530 in Q3 2022, reflecting scrap market fluctuations. Europe scrap costs were higher, eroding some margin gains. Energy costs increased in both regions, with Europe facing higher electricity prices amid the energy crisis but benefiting from hedging and Poland’s relatively less volatile rates.  
Controllable costs per ton rose modestly due to higher freight, energy, and alloy costs. Management attributed operational flexibility and cost leadership as key to managing these inflationary pressures.

### Commercial Strategy Insights

6. **Pricing and Backlog at Historically High Levels in North America; Europe Faces Uncertainty**  
Average selling price per ton for steel products in North America increased by \$204 year-over-year to \$888 per ton in Q4 2022, despite a \$6 decline from Q3 2022. Downstream products' average selling price increased by \$334 per ton year-over-year and \$104 sequentially. Contract backlog volumes and average pricing in North America reached historically high levels, supported by strong downstream bidding activity—an indicator of future construction project pipelines.  
The company noted continued strength in industrial end markets and construction-related demand in North America, boosted by structural trends such as the federal Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) with expected impacts starting in calendar 2023.  
Europe’s demand was mixed: Polish construction activity grew year-over-year, but industrial production in Central Europe contracted. Market uncertainty was heightened by the Ukraine war, energy crisis, and currency weakness (Polish Zloty). Import sanctions against Russia and Belarus were expected to tighten supply of long steel products in Central and Eastern Europe. Margins over scrap in both regions were expected to compress from Q4 levels due to increased supply of lower-priced imports and raw material price changes.

Margins on downstream products in North America expanded by \$231 per ton year-over-year, contributing to full value chain profitability above long-term averages. The downstream backlog grew year-over-year for the fifth consecutive quarter, with ongoing repricing of backlog contracts at higher price levels.  
The company’s value-added product lines, including construction-related fabricated steel and Tensar engineered solutions, enhanced product mix and commercial flexibility.  

### Market and Capacity Insights

8. **Strategic Growth Investments Include Tensar Acquisition and New Micro Mill Construction**  
CMC completed the acquisition of Tensar Corporation in late April 2022, adding engineered ground and soil stabilization solutions with global reach in over 80 national markets. Tensar’s acquisition was positioned as a profitable, less capital-intensive growth platform with potential commercial synergies and margin expansion.

### Corporate and Risk Insights

9. **European Energy Crisis and Geopolitical Risks Affect Operations; Company Benefits from Cost Leadership and Flexibility**  
The ongoing European energy crisis and the war in Ukraine created operational challenges including supply chain disruptions and increased energy costs. CMC’s Poland operations mitigated some impact through hedging and a low-cost operating structure relative to peers.  
The company acknowledged risks from fluctuating raw material costs, energy availability and pricing, currency volatility, and potential regulatory changes including environmental compliance and climate change regulations.  
CMC also disclosed risks related to competition, labor availability, information technology security, and potential legal and regulatory matters, consistent with industry norms.

### Wrap Up

Commercial Metals Company closed fiscal 2022 with record earnings and margins, driven by strong pricing, expanded downstream backlog, and operational execution across its North America and Europe segments. The Tensar acquisition contributed positively, broadening the company’s product portfolio and market reach. Despite increased raw material and energy costs, CMC managed inflationary pressures through operational flexibility and hedging strategies. North America entered fiscal 2023 with historically high contract backlogs and pricing, supported by structural demand drivers including federal infrastructure spending. Europe faced more mixed demand and margin compression risks due to geopolitical and energy challenges, though CMC’s cost position and recent capacity investments provided resilience. ### Wrap Up

In fiscal 2022, Commercial Metals Company delivered record financial results driven by strong pricing, expanded margins, and robust demand in North America, supported by a growing downstream backlog and positive bidding activity. Operationally, the company advanced key growth projects including the acquisition of Tensar Corporation and the Arizona 2 micro mill construction, enhancing capacity and product mix toward higher-margin finished steel products. Raw material and energy cost inflation exerted upward pressure on controllable costs, but margins over scrap remained at record levels, reflecting effective pricing and operational flexibility.

European operations faced challenges from geopolitical and energy market volatility but leveraged new rolling capacity and hedging strategies to maintain profitability. CMC maintained a strong balance sheet and liquidity position, enabling significant shareholder returns through dividends and share repurchases. The company’s sustainability initiatives and environmental targets further underscore its operational discipline. The fiscal year closed with CMC positioned for continued execution of its growth strategy amid a complex global steel market environment.

**Guidance:** For fiscal 2023, CMC anticipates continued strong North America demand supported by historically high backlog and bidding activity, with the Arizona 2 micro mill startup expected in early calendar 2023. European market conditions remain uncertain due to the energy crisis and industrial slowdown, but CMC expects to compete effectively due to cost leadership and operational flexibility. The commissioning of the Arizona 2 micro mill on schedule offers capacity growth and product mix flexibility to capitalize on favorable market trends.

   The Europe segment cut production by about 25% compared to the prior year period due to slowing Polish construction activity and muted industrial production in Central Europe. Shipments declined 9% year-over-year, which alongside margin compression, led to the segment's adjusted EBITDA loss [8-K 2023-10-12].

9. **Arizona 2 micro mill successfully started operations in June 2023 and is ramping production, adding expected annual capacity of 500,000 tons with flexibility between rebar and merchant bar.**  
   The Arizona 2 micro mill is expected to contribute to network optimization and capitalize on domestic rebar demand. The company recorded a \$15.7 million after-tax charge related to commissioning efforts in Q4 [8-K 2023-10-12, 8-K 2023-06-22].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

10. **Downstream new project bid volumes in North America grew by a double-digit percentage year-over-year in Q4, signaling a robust construction project pipeline despite a modest decline in downstream backlog volume and value.**  
    The increase in bid volumes supports a healthy demand outlook, although a slower conversion of bids into awards has reduced backlog compared to the prior year. This slowdown is attributed to tight labor markets and higher lending standards [8-K 2023-10-12].

11. **Tensar platform achieved record quarterly earnings contribution, supported by strong customer acceptance of new proprietary geogrid products.**  
    The growth in Tensar's profitability reflects successful innovation and market acceptance in ground and soil stabilization solutions, which complements CMC's steel reinforcement portfolio [8-K 2023-10-12].

12. **Integration of EDSCO Fasteners expanded CMC’s presence in electrical transmission anchoring solutions, broadening exposure to structural construction trends.**  
    This acquisition adds a new product line complementary to CMC’s existing construction reinforcement markets and is part of strategic growth initiatives including the Steel West Virginia project, which has commenced construction [8-K 2023-10-12].

### Market and Capacity Insights

13. **CMC’s extensive manufacturing network includes seven electric arc furnace (EAF) mini mills, two EAF micro mills including Arizona 2, and fabrication and recycling facilities principally in the U.S. and Poland.**  
    The company’s operations are organized into North America and Europe segments, serving a broad range of construction and industrial markets [10-K 2023-10-12, 8-K 2023-06-22].

    CMC continues to invest in growth and network optimization projects, supported by strong cash flow and disciplined capital allocation [8-K 2023-10-12].

### Corporate and Risk Insights

    The company repaid \$214 million in senior notes at maturity and repurchased \$116 million of senior notes through tender offers during fiscal 2023, supporting improved leverage and financial flexibility [8-K 2023-10-12].

### Wrap Up

In fiscal fourth quarter 2023, Commercial Metals Company experienced a notable decline in net earnings and net sales compared to the prior year, primarily driven by weaker European market conditions and margin compression. However, the North America segment showed resilience with a slight increase in adjusted EBITDA, supported by improved downstream product pricing and cost efficiencies despite lower steel product prices. Operationally, the successful start-up of the Arizona 2 micro mill and strong demand signals from increased downstream bid volumes underpin the company’s strategic growth initiatives. The Europe segment remains challenged by demand softness and energy cost inflation, though government rebates are expected to partially mitigate these pressures in fiscal 2024.

CMC’s robust cash flow generation and disciplined capital allocation enabled continued share repurchases, dividend payments, and debt reduction, maintaining a strong liquidity position. Strategic acquisitions and investments, including the integration of EDSCO Fasteners and progress on the Steel West Virginia project, broaden the company’s product and market exposure. The company expects first quarter fiscal 2024 performance to decline sequentially due to seasonal factors, margin compression in North America, and ongoing European challenges, with government rebates providing some offset.

**Guidance Overview:**  
Management anticipates continued strong financial performance by historical standards in the near term but expects a sequential decline in Q1 fiscal 2024 due to seasonally lower shipments and margin pressures. Downstream product prices increased \$81 per ton, helping offset some margin pressure [8-K 2023-10-12].  
   In contrast, Europe shipments declined 9% year-over-year in Q4 FY23 amid weakening end-market demand, including slower Polish construction and contracting industrial production in Central Europe [8-K 2023-10-12]. European adjusted EBITDA swung to a loss of \$25.7 million from a \$64.1 million profit in the prior year quarter, driven by metal margin erosion and volume declines [8-K 2023-10-12]. The startup coincided with growing construction activity fueled by infrastructure spending and reshoring trends [8-K 2023-06-22]. Operational startup costs related to Arizona 2 contributed to a \$15.7 million net after-tax charge in Q4 FY23 [8-K 2023-10-12].

   Controllable costs per ton of finished steel decreased compared to the prior year period in Q4 FY23, driven primarily by lower input costs for key consumables and reduced freight rates, which more than offset increased costs related to the Arizona 2 startup and a planned outage at the Steel Alabama merchant bar mill [8-K 2023-10-12]. However, fiscal Q3 FY23 saw a 6% increase in controllable costs per ton year-over-year due to inflationary pressures [8-K 2023-06-22].

   CMC’s downstream backlog volume and value remained near all-time highs throughout fiscal 2023, with new project bid volumes in North America growing by a double-digit percentage year-over-year in Q4 FY23 [8-K 2023-10-12; 8-K 2023-06-22]. This backlog provides revenue visibility and helps stabilize earnings despite steel product margin volatility [8-K 2023-06-22; 8-K 2023-01-09].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

   While average selling prices for steel products declined in fiscal 2023, downstream products saw price increases (e.g., \$81 per ton higher in Q4 FY23 versus prior year) and contributed to expanded margins over scrap on downstream products [8-K 2023-10-12; 8-K 2023-06-22]. The company’s ability to optimize product mix and leverage downstream fabrication supports margin stability amid raw material price fluctuations [8-K 2023-06-22].

9. **Strategic Acquisitions and Growth Projects Expand Market Reach and Product Offerings**  
   CMC completed six bolt-on acquisitions totaling \$235 million in fiscal 2023, broadening its commercial portfolio and strengthening operations [8-K 2023-10-12]. The acquisition of Tensar, a provider of engineered ground stabilization solutions, has extended CMC’s exposure to infrastructure markets and added a high-margin growth platform [8-K 2023-01-09; 8-K 2023-06-22].  
   Construction commenced on the Steel West Virginia micro mill, projected to add 500,000 tons of capacity and improve geographic reach in the Eastern U.S. with an expected startup in late 2025 [8-K 2023-01-09; 8-K 2023-06-22].

### Market and Capacity Insights

10. **Capacity Expansion Balances with Production Reductions in Europe to Manage Inventory and Demand**  
    CMC’s network includes seven electric arc furnace (EAF) mini mills and two EAF micro mills in the U.S. and Poland [10-K 2023-10-12]. The commissioning of Arizona 2 and the planned Steel West Virginia micro mill represent significant capacity additions [8-K 2023-06-22; 8-K 2023-01-09].  
    In Europe, production was reduced by about 25% in Q4 FY23 to align with weaker demand and inventory levels [8-K 2023-10-12]. The addition of a third rolling line in Europe, commissioned in mid-2021, has increased operational flexibility and allowed CMC to convert more material to finished product, enhancing margins and market share despite volatile market conditions [8-K 2023-03-23; 8-K 2022-10-13].

### Corporate and Risk Insights

11. **Energy Cost Inflation and Government Rebate Programs Affect European Segment Profitability**  
    European operations faced margin pressure due to rising energy costs and softer demand, with the segment reporting an adjusted EBITDA loss in Q4 FY23 [8-K 2023-10-12]. However, CMC expects approximately \$60 million in government rebates during Q1 FY24 from CO2 credits and energy cost reimbursements by the Polish government, which should improve European segment adjusted EBITDA [8-K 2023-10-12].

12. **Exposure to Import Competition and Trade Policy Risks Persist**  
    CMC acknowledges that global steel capacity exceeds demand in some regions, creating import competition risks [10-K 2023-10-12]. The company benefits from U.S. trade enforcement laws such as Section 232 tariffs but notes these may be temporary, and import competition remains a significant threat [10-K 2023-10-12].

### Wrap Up

In fiscal 2023, Commercial Metals Company experienced a decline in net earnings and adjusted EBITDA from the record highs of 2022, primarily due to margin compression and weaker European market conditions. North America remained resilient with stable shipments, supported by a strong downstream backlog and the operational startup of the Arizona 2 micro mill, which adds flexible, low-cost capacity. Europe faced volume declines and margin erosion amid energy cost inflation and subdued industrial demand, partially offset by expected government rebates.

The company maintained disciplined capital allocation, continuing share repurchases, increasing dividends, and reducing debt, supported by strong free cash flow generation. Strategic growth initiatives, including acquisitions and the development of the Steel West Virginia micro mill, position CMC to capitalize on infrastructure-driven demand and reshoring trends. Risks from import competition and volatile energy costs remain relevant, particularly in Europe, but government programs and CMC’s operational flexibility provide some mitigation.

**Guidance Overview:**  
Management expects continued strong financial performance by historical standards in Q1 FY24 but anticipates a sequential decline from Q4 FY23 due to seasonal shipment reductions, steel product margin compression in North America, and ongoing European market challenges. The European segment is projected to benefit from approximately \$60 million in government rebates tied to CO2 credits and energy cost reimbursements [8-K 2023-10-12]. No specific quantitative guidance ranges were disclosed.

### Wrap Up

Commercial Metals Company’s fiscal second quarter of 2024 featured a significant decline in net and adjusted earnings driven by commissioning costs at the Arizona 2 micro mill and compressed steel product margins, despite an increase in North American steel shipments and a rebound in downstream contract awards signaling a strong construction pipeline. Europe Steel Group’s market conditions improved sequentially, reducing losses, while Emerging Businesses faced weather and project delays that pressured profitability despite modest sales growth and acquisitions. The company maintained a strong liquidity position, increased dividends, and continued share repurchases, supporting its capital allocation strategy alongside ongoing growth investments.

### Wrap Up

Commercial Metals Company’s fiscal Q3 2024 results reflect a mix of stable operational activity and strategic investments amid a challenging pricing and margin environment. Emerging Businesses Group maintained margins supported by acquisitions and proprietary product demand, offset by weather-related delays. The adjusted EBITDA margin for this group declined to 13.5% in Q4 from 14.7% in Q3 and 19.6% a year earlier [8-K 2024-10-17; 8-K 2024-06-20].

   CMC generated \$351.8 million of cash flow from operating activities in Q4 and \$899.7 million for fiscal 2024, down from \$1.3 billion in 2023. Quarterly dividends were maintained at \$0.18 per share, marking the 240th consecutive quarterly dividend payment [8-K 2024-10-17].

### Operations Insights

5. **Stable North American shipment volumes with pressure on margins due to pricing and commissioning costs**  
   Finished steel shipments in North America were stable in Q4 2024, with average daily shipments virtually unchanged year-over-year and sequentially. However, adjusted EBITDA per ton of finished steel shipped declined from \$294 in Q4 2023 to \$188 in Q4 2024, driven by a \$72 per ton decrease in steel product margins over scrap and an \$86 per ton decline in downstream product margins. Commissioning costs related to the Arizona 2 micro mill increased to \$15.1 million in Q4 from \$12.3 million a year ago, further pressuring earnings [8-K 2024-10-17].

The segment faced flat margins over scrap, with an \$8 per ton margin reduction sequentially, offset by higher shipment volumes and lower controllable costs. Despite some positive demand trends in Poland and regional supply discipline, increased imports weighed on results. Long-steel consumption remained below historical levels [8-K 2024-10-17].

7. **Emerging Businesses Group delivered record profitability driven by Tensar**

Tensar, a key division within this group, drove this performance with strong demand for high-margin construction solutions such as geogrids and proprietary reinforcing steel products. The group’s net sales were stable year-over-year, supported by the acquisition of CMC Anchoring Systems, partially offset by declines in CMC Construction Services due to lower selling prices and weather-related delays [8-K 2024-10-17; 10-K 2024-10-17; 10-Q 2024-06-25].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

However, bid volumes declined from the peaks of fiscal 2022 and 2023, and some projects were reportedly on hold amid macroeconomic and political uncertainty, including interest rate and election outcomes. The company emphasized its long-term structural trends—such as infrastructure investment, re-shoring, electrification, and housing shortages—as underpinning future demand [8-K 2024-10-17].

   Shipments of merchant products (merchant bar quality, MBQ) increased year-over-year in Q4 2024, attributed to improved service capability from the Arizona 2 micro mill. This facility’s commissioning costs increased but is positioned to support market presence and cost competitiveness [8-K 2024-10-17].

The company is targeting growth capital expenditures on key mill projects aimed at strengthening market presence and lowering costs. No acquisitions were completed in fiscal 2024, though the company remains focused on disciplined capital allocation including operational capability expansion and commercial portfolio enhancement [8-K 2024-10-17; 8-K 2024-06-20].

Financially, CMC generated strong operating cash flows and increased shareholder returns through dividends and share repurchases, while capital expenditures rose, reflecting investments in mill expansions and growth projects expected to support future cost competitiveness. 2025.Q2:
### Financial Insights

1. **Net earnings declined sharply year-over-year amid margin compression in North America Steel Group**  
   For the fiscal second quarter ended February 28, 2025, CMC reported net earnings of \$25.5 million (\$0.22 per diluted share), down from \$85.8 million in the prior year quarter. Adjusted earnings were \$29.3 million (\$0.26 per diluted share) compared to \$85.9 million a year earlier. Consolidated core EBITDA dropped to \$131.0 million with a 7.5% margin, down from \$212.1 million and 11.5% margin in Q2 FY24. The North America Steel Group’s adjusted EBITDA fell to \$128.8 million from \$222.3 million, with a margin decline from 15.0% to 9.3%. This earnings contraction was attributed primarily to lower steel product margins over scrap costs and downstream product margin declines, despite stable shipments and controlled costs. The quarter also included about \$8 million in unrealized losses on copper hedging positions [8-K 2025-03-20; 10-Q 2025-03-25].

2. **Strong cash generation supports aggressive share repurchases and dividend continuity**  
   CMC ended Q2 FY25 with \$758.4 million in cash and cash equivalents and nearly \$1.6 billion in total liquidity. During the quarter, the company repurchased 906,603 shares for \$48.0 million, increasing share repurchases by 84% year-over-year on a 12-month basis to \$205 million, representing 3.3% of shares outstanding. The board declared a quarterly dividend of \$0.18 per share, marking the 242nd consecutive quarterly dividend payment, with a payout ratio of 16% in FY24. The company had \$305.3 million remaining under its current share repurchase authorization as of February 28, 2025 [8-K 2025-03-20; 10-Q 2025-03-25].

3. **Capital expenditures remain elevated with a focus on organic growth and cost reduction projects**  
   CMC’s capital expenditures for the first half of FY25 totaled \$204.5 million, with full-year guidance of \$550 million to \$600 million. Approximately \$250 million to \$300 million of FY25 capex relates to the Steel West Virginia project. Investments focus on key mill projects to strengthen market presence, reduce costs, and expand proprietary early-stage construction solutions. No acquisitions were completed in FY24 or YTD FY25, but the company maintains a disciplined approach targeting value-accretive growth opportunities [8-K 2025-03-20].

### Operations Insights

4. **Finished steel shipments grew 3.3% year-over-year, driven by resilient North American construction demand**  
   CMC shipped 1.044 million external finished steel tons in Q2 FY25 in the North America Steel Group, up from 1.010 million tons in Q2 FY24. The increase was supported by healthy downstream project awards and a nearly 10% sequential increase in backlog volumes from Q1 FY25, stable year-over-year. Europe Steel Group shipped 310,000 tons, slightly down from 319,000 tons a year earlier but improved sequentially. The Emerging Businesses Group’s shipments were flat overall, with a notable 86% increase in performance reinforcing steel volumes offset by weaker Impact Metals shipments due to a slowing truck and trailer market [8-K 2025-03-20; 10-Q 2025-03-25].

5. **Steel product margins over scrap declined \$50 per ton year-over-year in North America, with downstream product margins down about \$117 per ton**  
   The North America Steel Group’s steel product metal margin per ton fell from \$275 in Q2 FY24 to \$225 (derived from \$50/ton decline). Downstream product margins over scrap remained above historical levels but dropped by approximately \$117 per ton. Controllable costs per ton were flat year-over-year due to successful cost management offsetting weather-related operational disruptions. Europe Steel Group’s steel product metal margin per ton was stable around \$279, supported by a \$4 million natural gas cost rebate and reduced scrap costs, leading to adjusted EBITDA breakeven compared to a prior year loss [8-K 2025-03-20].

6. **Raw material cost volatility influenced pricing and margins, with scrap prices rising early in the quarter prompting product price increases**  
   Domestic scrap prices increased in January and February 2025, leading CMC to raise prices on primary steel products. Imported rebar supply remained modest relative to long-term averages despite a temporary surge in January ahead of tariff considerations. Steel product average selling prices in North America ended the quarter higher than the December 2024 low, supporting margin stabilization late in the quarter. Europe benefited from reduced Polish rebar imports, improving supply-demand balance and allowing domestic price stabilization [8-K 2025-03-20].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

7. **North American market saw improved downstream bidding and second highest new contract awards since late FY22**  
   The company noted a healthy pipeline for future construction projects, with new contract awards in Q2 FY25 reaching the second highest level since late fiscal 2022. This contributed to a stable year-over-year backlog and a nearly 10% sequential backlog increase from Q1 FY25. Merchant bar and other product shipments grew, aided by increased capacity from the Arizona 2 micro mill serving West Coast customers. The company emphasized its ongoing commercial discipline and operational excellence program (TAG) as key to supporting margins amid economic uncertainty [8-K 2025-03-20].

8. **Emerging Businesses Group profitability improved 31.2% year-over-year on strong shipments and higher-margin product mix**  
   Net sales for the Emerging Businesses Group were \$158.9 million, up 1.8% year-over-year, while adjusted EBITDA rose to \$23.5 million from \$17.9 million in Q2 FY24. The performance reinforcing steel business drove gains with increased shipments of proprietary corrosion-resistant products. Other divisions such as Tensar and Construction Services remained largely flat, while Impact Metals declined modestly due to weaker truck and trailer demand. The segment’s adjusted EBITDA margin improved by 330 basis points to 14.8% [8-K 2025-03-20].

### Market and Capacity Insights

9. **Micro mill investments and reshoring initiatives continue to support strategic growth and cost reduction**  
   CMC placed its third micro mill into service in Q4 FY23 and continues to commission related operational costs through FY25. The Arizona 2 micro mill increased merchant bar shipments, particularly serving West Coast customers. Capital investments, including the Steel West Virginia project, aim to strengthen market presence and reduce costs. The company’s strategic transformation over recent years includes reshoring critical manufacturing and expanding proprietary early-stage construction solutions [8-K 2025-03-20].

### Corporate and Risk Insights

10. **Legal contingencies and hedging losses impacted financial results and balance sheet**  
    The quarter’s results included \$8 million in unrealized losses on financial positions hedging CMC’s physical copper exposure. Additionally, the balance sheet as of February 28, 2025, included a \$354.7 million accrued contingent litigation-related loss not present at August 31, 2024, indicating ongoing legal risk. Long-term debt remained stable at approximately \$1.15 billion, and the company reported compliance with all credit covenant requirements [8-K 2025-03-20; 10-Q 2025-03-25].

### Wrap Up

In Q2 FY25, Commercial Metals Company faced significant margin pressure in its North America Steel Group, driving a sharp decline in net earnings despite a 3.3% increase in finished steel shipments supported by resilient construction demand and a strong project backlog. The Europe Steel Group returned to adjusted EBITDA breakeven aided by cost controls and energy rebates, while the Emerging Businesses Group posted higher profitability driven by performance reinforcing steel. Raw material price volatility, especially scrap costs, influenced pricing and margins, with improvements in market conditions late in the quarter. CMC maintained strong liquidity, enabling increased share repurchases and a continuing quarterly dividend streak. Capital expenditures remained elevated, focused on organic growth and cost reduction projects like Steel West Virginia and micro mill expansions. Legal contingencies and hedging losses added to financial headwinds but did not impair covenant compliance.

**Guidance Overview:**  
CMC anticipates a sequential rebound in Q3 FY25 financial results, expecting North America Steel Group shipments to follow typical seasonal patterns and adjusted EBITDA margins to improve on higher margins over scrap. Europe Steel Group adjusted EBITDA is projected near or slightly above breakeven, benefiting from ongoing cost management. Emerging Businesses Group financials are expected to modestly exceed prior year levels. Capital expenditure guidance for FY25 remains at \$550 million to \$600 million, underscoring a continued focus on growth and efficiency investments [8-K 2025-03-20].
2025.Q3:
### Financial Insights

1. **Third quarter net earnings declined to \$83.1 million from \$119.4 million year-over-year, reflecting lower steel product margins despite higher shipments.**  
   For Q3 FY 2025 ended May 31, net earnings were \$83.1 million (\$0.73 per diluted share), down from \$119.4 million (\$1.02 per diluted share) in Q3 FY 2024 on net sales of \$2.02 billion versus \$2.08 billion. Adjusted earnings were \$84.4 million (\$0.74 per diluted share). Consolidated core EBITDA was \$204.1 million with a 10.1% margin, down from prior year levels. The decline was driven by reduced margins over scrap costs in the North America Steel Group despite a 1.6% increase in finished steel shipments year-over-year and a 10.4% sequential shipment increase reflecting seasonality [8-K 2025-06-23; 10-Q 2025-06-24].

2. **North America Steel Group adjusted EBITDA fell 24.4% year-over-year to \$186.0 million with margin compression from 14.7% to 11.9%, despite TAG program benefits and higher shipments.**  
   Adjusted EBITDA decreased from \$246.3 million in Q3 FY 2024 to \$186.0 million in Q3 FY 2025, with margin declining from 14.7% to 11.9%. This was primarily due to a \$39 per ton drop in steel product metal margins over scrap and a \$77 per ton decline in downstream product margins over scrap, partially offset by benefits from the Transform, Advance, Grow (TAG) program initiatives such as melt shop and rolling mill yield improvements, scrap cost optimization, logistics, and alloy consumption reduction. Shipments of finished steel products increased 1.6% year-over-year and 10.4% sequentially [8-K 2025-06-23; 10-Q 2025-06-24].

3. **Emerging Businesses Group grew adjusted EBITDA 7.0% year-over-year to \$40.9 million on a 4.7% rise in net sales, driven by strong shipments and higher-margin proprietary reinforcing steel products.**  
   Segment net sales rose from \$188.6 million to \$197.5 million, with adjusted EBITDA margin improving 40 basis points to 20.7%, the second highest on record. Growth was mainly attributed to Performance Reinforcing Steel shipments and product mix, while Tensar’s profitability declined modestly due to project delays. Construction Services and Impact Metals results were largely flat year-over-year [8-K 2025-06-23; 10-Q 2025-06-24].

4. **Europe Steel Group returned to profitability with adjusted EBITDA of \$3.6 million and a positive margin of 1.5%, supported by improved market fundamentals and cost management.**  
   The segment’s shipments increased 20.9% year-over-year to 359,000 tons, with steel product metal margins over scrap up modestly from the prior year and sequential quarter. Pricing exited Q3 at approximately \$70 per ton above the December low. Cost controls contributed to earnings gains despite ongoing market challenges. The group benefited from reduced import flows and solid Polish economic conditions [8-K 2025-06-23].

5. **Cash and liquidity remained strong with \$893 million in cash and equivalents and over \$1.7 billion in available liquidity; \$50.4 million spent on share repurchases in Q3 with \$254.9 million remaining authorization.**  
   The company repurchased 1.1 million shares at an average price of \$45.30 per share during the quarter. Dividend payments totaled \$61.3 million for the first nine months of FY 2025, maintaining the 243rd consecutive quarterly dividend at \$0.18 per share. Debt increased modestly to \$1.3 billion long-term, and the company remained in compliance with all credit covenants [8-K 2025-06-23; 10-Q 2025-06-24].

6. **Capital expenditures reached \$293.9 million through the first nine months of FY 2025, with full-year guidance of \$425 million to \$475 million; no new mill investments planned.**  
   The company expects to complete its low-cost, flexible mill network with the Steel West Virginia project. Future organic growth will focus on high-return opportunities in proprietary early-stage construction solutions. No acquisitions were made in FY 2024 or YTD FY 2025, with a disciplined approach targeting \$500 million to \$750 million in transaction value for inorganic growth aligned with strategic goals [8-K 2025-06-23].

### Operations Insights

7. **Steel product metal margins in North America inflected upward sequentially, increasing \$23 per ton during Q3 and exiting above the \$499 per ton average for the period, driven by selling price gains exceeding scrap cost increases.**  
   Compared to Q2 FY 2025, average selling prices for steel products rose \$45 per ton, outpacing a \$22 per ton rise in scrap costs. Despite meaningful scrap price reductions in April and May, CMC maintained price levels achieved earlier in the year, contributing to improved metal margins [8-K 2025-06-23].

8. **Finished steel shipments in North America increased 1.6% year-over-year to 1.15 million tons and 10.4% sequentially, reflecting normal seasonality and solid demand, supported by a healthy pipeline of construction projects.**  
   The stable downstream backlog and bidding activity, along with the Dodge Momentum Index indicating strong project planning, underpin expectations for continued shipment levels in the 2025 construction season. Merchant bar shipments grew due to expanded capacity from the Arizona 2 micro mill serving West Coast customers [8-K 2025-06-23].

9. **Europe Steel Group shipments rose 20.9% year-over-year to 359,000 tons, supported by improved market balance and reduced import competition, with steel product prices increasing approximately \$70 per ton since December lows.**  
   The segment’s cost management efforts yielded year-over-year EBITDA improvements despite modest metal margin gains. The company expects a \$28 million CO2 credit related to Polish energy cost rebates in Q4 FY 2025, with the second tranche expected in Q1 FY 2026 [8-K 2025-06-23].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

10. **CMC’s TAG program is exceeding targeted EBITDA benefits with an expected annual run-rate exceeding \$100 million, driving margin, cash flow, and return on capital improvements across segments.**  
    TAG initiatives focus on operational efficiencies such as yield enhancement, scrap cost optimization, and logistics improvements. Management emphasized the program as a key pillar of strategy to improve performance and enable disciplined capital allocation [8-K 2025-06-23].

11. **Emerging Businesses Group’s growth centers on proprietary, high-margin products like Performance Reinforcing Steel, with the segment targeting expansion in early-stage construction markets valued at approximately \$150 billion.**  
    CMC is investing in organic growth and pursuing inorganic opportunities to extend its portfolio in early-stage construction solutions, including soil stabilization, anchoring systems, and engineered reinforcing products. Project quotes and planning activity remain healthy, supporting future shipment growth [8-K 2025-06-23].

### Market and Capacity Insights

12. **No new steel mill investments are planned in the foreseeable future; focus remains on completing the Steel West Virginia mill to finalize a low-cost, flexible mill network.**  
    Capital allocation priorities emphasize sustaining the existing network and investing in automation and process efficiency rather than greenfield mill expansions. This supports a disciplined approach to growth and capital deployment [8-K 2025-06-23].

### Corporate and Risk Insights

13. **Trade policy changes, including elimination of Section 232 tariff exemptions and rate increases to 50%, have restricted imports reaching the U.S., supporting domestic mill utilization but increasing uncertainty on future project costs and material availability.**  
    CMC sources primarily from domestic suppliers, limiting outage risk, and major equipment for large organic projects has already been received, reducing tariff exposure on capital costs. The company anticipates modest cost impact from tariffs with potential for decline [8-K 2025-06-23].

14. **Legal and tax items impacted non-operational results with \$3.8 million interest expense estimated on PSG litigation and a \$2.8 million credit from settlement of New Markets Tax Credit transactions in Q3.**  
    These items affected pre-tax earnings but are disclosed separately from core operating performance [8-K 2025-06-23].

### Wrap Up

Commercial Metals Company’s Q3 FY 2025 results illustrate a complex operational environment with improving steel product prices and shipments supporting sequential margin gains but not fully offsetting year-over-year margin compression, especially in the North America Steel Group. The TAG program continues to contribute meaningfully to cost and yield improvements, partially mitigating margin pressures. Emerging Businesses Group demonstrated solid growth driven by proprietary products, while Europe Steel Group returned to profitability amid better market conditions and cost controls. Strong liquidity and disciplined capital spending underpin CMC’s strategy to complete its mill network and pursue targeted growth in early-stage construction solutions. Trade policy developments and legal contingencies add layers of risk and cost considerations, though capital expenditures and acquisitions remain controlled.

**Guidance Overview:**  
CMC expects Q4 FY 2025 consolidated financial results to improve sequentially on higher steel product margins and seasonal shipment patterns. Emerging Businesses Group results are projected to improve both sequentially and year-over-year. Europe Steel Group anticipates receiving a \$28 million CO2 credit in Q4 and expects adjusted EBITDA to increase sequentially excluding this credit, supported by ongoing market and cost improvements [8-K 2025-06-23].

8. **North America Steel Group shipments of finished steel products rose 3.0% year-over-year and were flat sequentially, with merchant product shipments growing due to increased service capability from the Arizona 2 micro mill, which generated positive adjusted EBITDA in Q4.** Downstream backlog volumes declined mid-single digits year-over-year due to more disciplined commercial selectivity focused on project margin goals and risk profile, but backlog remains historically well-sized to support future shipments [8-K 2025-10-16].

11. **The TAG (Transform, Advance, Grow) program exceeded targeted EBITDA benefits in fiscal 2025, delivering operational improvements such as melt shop and rolling mill yield enhancements, scrap cost optimization, logistics efficiencies, and reduced alloy consumption, contributing significantly to margin expansion and cash flow [8-K 2025-10-16; 8-K 2025-06-23].**

### Commercial Strategy Insights

12. **CMC’s commercial strategy focused on expanding its early-stage construction solutions portfolio, evidenced by acquisitions of Foley and CP&P, which broaden the precast concrete product offering and enable earlier participation on construction job sites.** The acquisitions are expected to generate commercial synergies by increasing interactions with key decision makers and expanding CMC’s wallet share across multiple construction phases [8-K 2025-09-18; 8-K 2025-10-16].

13. **Downstream bidding activity and the Dodge Momentum Index indicated a healthy pipeline of potential future construction projects, though CMC adopted more disciplined commercial selectivity to manage project margin and risk, resulting in a mid-single digit decline in downstream backlog volumes year-over-year.** This backlog remains sufficient to support steel shipments in coming quarters [8-K 2025-10-16].

### Corporate and Risk Insights

14. **CMC recorded an after-tax litigation charge of approximately \$274 million in fiscal 2025 related to the Pacific Steel Group v. Commercial Metals Co. case, with an adverse ruling upheld in September 2025 and plans to appeal.** An accrued contingent litigation-related loss of \$362.3 million was recognized on the balance sheet as of August 31, 2025 [10-K 2025-10-16; 8-K 2025-09-30; 8-K 2025-10-16].

15. **Trade policy developments, including elimination of Section 232 tariff exemptions and increased tariffs to 50%, along with trade cases against certain countries, have restricted imports into the U.S., supporting domestic pricing and market conditions.** CMC sources primarily from domestic suppliers, limiting exposure to tariff-related cost disruptions. The policy environment is expected to encourage U.S. manufacturing investment [8-K 2025-06-23; 8-K 2025-10-16].

16. **CMC’s balance sheet reflected increased current liabilities to \$1.26 billion at August 31, 2025, from \$835 million a year earlier, driven in part by the accrued contingent litigation loss.** Long-term debt rose to \$1.31 billion from \$1.15 billion, aligned with recent acquisitions and capital projects. Stockholders’ equity decreased slightly to \$4.19 billion from \$4.30 billion [8-K 2025-10-16].

---

### Wrap Up

In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, Commercial Metals Company showed marked improvement in earnings and margins, led by expanding steel product metal margins in North America, record profitability in the Emerging Businesses Group, and a strong rebound in the Europe Steel Group aided by a government CO2 credit. The TAG program contributed operational efficiencies that supported margin expansion and cash flow. Shipments grew modestly, supported by a healthy construction pipeline, though backlog declined slightly due to more selective project bidding.

Strategically, CMC advanced its portfolio through acquisitions of Foley and CP&P, establishing a scaled precast concrete platform that broadens early-stage construction participation and is expected to enhance margins and cash flow. The company maintained a strong liquidity position, continued share repurchases, and sustained its dividend record. However, fiscal 2025 results were weighed down by a significant litigation charge, with related contingent liabilities recognized and ongoing appeals planned. Trade policies restricting imports have supported domestic pricing, with no reported material operational disruptions from tariffs.

**Guidance Overview:** While explicit forward guidance for fiscal 2026 was not included in the excerpts, management expressed optimism that the recent Federal Reserve interest rate reductions and a robust construction pipeline will support continued performance improvements. Fiscal 2026 capital expenditures are projected at approximately \$600 million to complete organic growth projects, with an emphasis on deleveraging from recent acquisitions within 18 months. No other specific risks or events were disclosed as imminent beyond ongoing litigation and regulatory reviews of acquisitions.

    Downstream backlog volumes in North America declined by a mid-single digit percentage year-over-year in Q4 FY25 due to more disciplined commercial selectivity focused on project margin goals and risk profile, despite stable or growing shipment volumes and a healthy pipeline of future construction projects [8-K 2025-10-16; 8-K 2025-06-23; 8-K 2025-03-20]. The Dodge Momentum Index, which tracks projects entering the planning phase, remained at record or healthy levels across the year, indicating sustained early-stage construction demand [8-K 2025-10-16; 8-K 2025-06-23].

    After margin compression in the first half of the fiscal year, the steel pricing environment improved in the second half, with average selling prices rising and scrap costs declining, driving margin expansion [8-K 2025-06-23; 8-K 2025-10-16]. Domestic scrap pricing increased in early 2025, prompting steel product price increases, while import rebar supply remained modest relative to longer-term averages, supporting domestic pricing [8-K 2025-03-20].

### Labor Insights

12. **Safety Performance Reached Near-Record Levels Across Operational Footprint**  
    CMC reported near-record safety performance during fiscal 2025, achieving world-class safety metrics across all segments and continuing a multi-year trend of improving total recordable incident rates [8-K 2025-06-23; 8-K 2025-10-16]. This focus on safety was highlighted as a core mission and a foundation for operational effectiveness [8-K 2025-06-23].

### Wrap Up

Fiscal 2025 was marked by a significant net earnings decline primarily due to a large litigation charge but also reflected ongoing margin pressures early in the year. However, CMC’s operational and commercial excellence program (TAG) delivered financial benefits exceeding expectations, contributing to margin recovery and cost reductions. The North America Steel Group saw steady shipment growth and margin improvement in the second half, while the Europe Steel Group returned to profitability through cost management and improved market conditions. The Emerging Businesses Group posted record results, supported by strong demand for Tensar and Performance Reinforcing Steel products. The Arizona 2 micro mill became a positive contributor, expanding merchant product shipments on the West Coast.

Commercial discipline led to a modest decline in backlog volumes but was balanced by a healthy pipeline of future construction projects. Capital expenditures focused on growth projects and operational improvements, while acquisitions of Foley and CP&P were announced post-year-end to expand CMC’s commercial portfolio and scale. The company maintained strong liquidity, continued share repurchases, and sustained dividend payments. Safety performance remained a key priority with near-record results.

**Guidance and Outlook:**  
No explicit forward guidance for fiscal 2026 was disclosed in the filings. However, management expressed optimism about converting pent-up demand into activity in fiscal 2026, supported by expected Fed interest rate reductions and ongoing structural demand trends in construction [8-K 2025-10-16]. The TAG program is expected to continue generating financial benefits beyond fiscal 2025 [8-K 2025-06-23]. No material risks beyond the litigation charge and normal market uncertainties were newly disclosed.

### Financial Insights

2. **Net Sales Slightly Decreased Despite Volume Growth in Some Segments**  
   Total net sales were \$3.545 billion in Q2 2019, a 2% decrease from \$3.609 billion in Q2 2018. The Flat-Rolled segment’s sales grew 4% due to increased shipments (+220 thousand net tons), mainly hot rolled and semi-finished products. US Steel Europe (USSE) sales declined 20% due to lower shipments (-152 thousand net tons), currency headwinds (weaker euro), and import competition. Tubular sales increased 2% driven by higher prices (+\$75/ton) partially offset by lower shipments (-6 thousand net tons) [10-Q 2019-08-02; 8-K 2019-08-01].

3. **Capital Expenditures Increased Substantially, Focused on Strategic and Environmental Projects**  
   Capital expenditures totaled \$326 million in Q2 2019, up from \$173 million in Q2 2018. Flat-Rolled segment capex was \$254 million, including spending on the Mon Valley No. 3 Blast Furnace outage, Gary Hot Strip Mill upgrades, Great Lakes B2 Blast Furnace outage, and other infrastructure and environmental projects. USSE and Tubular segments spent \$41 million and \$29 million, respectively, on emission controls, new production lines, and strategic projects. Contractual commitments for property, plant, and equipment were \$820 million as of June 30, 2019 [10-Q 2019-08-02].

4. **Cash and Liquidity Remain Strong with \$651 Million in Cash and \$2.48 Billion Total Liquidity**  
   As of June 30, 2019, U.S. Steel held \$651 million in cash and cash equivalents and had \$2.48 billion in total liquidity, including \$1.5 billion available under a credit facility and \$329 million under USSK credit facilities. ### Operations Insights

5. **Production Capacity Reduced by Idling Blast Furnaces to Align with Market Demand**  
   In June 2019, U.S. Steel idled two U.S. blast furnaces and one in Europe, reducing monthly blast furnace capacity by approximately 200,000–225,000 tons in the U.S. and 125,000 tons in Europe. This was intended to better align global production with the order book. Restart of idled furnaces is possible when market conditions improve [10-Q 2019-08-02].

6. **Raw Steel Production and Shipments Show Mixed Trends Across Segments**  
   Flat-Rolled raw steel production increased 5% year-over-year to 2.984 million net tons in Q2 2019, with capability utilization rising to 70% from 67%. Shipments increased 9% to 2.804 million net tons. Conversely, USSE raw steel production decreased 12% to 1.148 million net tons, with utilization falling to 92% from 105%, and shipments declined 13% to 1.004 million net tons. Tubular production and shipments decreased slightly (-3% and -5%) [8-K 2019-08-01; 10-Q 2019-08-02].

   Flat-Rolled segment EBITDA was \$244 million in Q2 2019, down from \$316 million in Q2 2018. The decline was driven by lower average realized prices (-\$36 million impact), higher raw material costs due to coal and purchased coke (+\$39 million unfavorable), and increased maintenance and outage costs (+\$42 million), reflecting planned asset revitalization outages. USSE segment EBITDA fell sharply to \$13 million from \$136 million, impacted by lower prices, volumes, higher iron ore costs (+\$52 million), and adverse currency effects. Tubular segment EBITDA was \$6 million, down from a loss of \$23 million in Q2 2018 but lower than Q1 2019 due to restart and investment-related costs [8-K 2019-08-01; 10-Q 2019-08-02].
